articles.title: When Digital Exposure Meets Everyday Buying: Understanding Consumer Behaviour in FMCG
articles.abstract: Consumers today may discover a product on social media, encounter it repeatedly through digital advertising, and still make the final purchase from a neighbourhood store. This study explores the relationship between digital exposure and everyday consumer behaviour in the fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG) sector. Using a consumer survey dataset containing 26 usable responses, the study examines purchase frequency, purchase channels, exposure to social-media promotions, reported influence of online advertising, customer satisfaction, and recommendation intention. The findings show that social-media exposure is relatively common, while reported influence of online advertising is more mixed. Traditional retail remains important, with kirana stores and supermarkets accounting for most reported purchase channels. Mean satisfaction was 3.92 out of 5 among respondents with valid satisfaction scores, while recommendation intention was predominantly positive. Exploratory statistical analysis did not identify a statistically significant association between online-ad influence and recommendation intention (χ² = 0.26, p = 0.61), nor a statistically significant relationship between satisfaction and recommendation intention (Spearman ρ ≈ 0.21, p ≈ 0.31). The findings suggest that digital visibility should not automatically be interpreted as behavioural influence. Consumer decisions appear to involve a broader combination of digital communication, product experience, purchasing convenience, availability, and customer service. Given the small and youth-concentrated sample, the study is exploratory and does not claim population-level generalizability. The paper highlights the need for larger and more diverse studies examining how digital engagement interacts with the wider FMCG consumer journey.

articles.title: Human Circuits in Cold War Taiwan: RCA, Labour Governance, and the Developmental State
articles.abstract: Industrial development depends on institutions that organise technological learning and govern production. In Cold War Taiwan, these institutions also shaped who could challenge industrial harm. Drawing on field research, interviews, legal records, and institutional histories, this article argues that Taiwan’s developmental capacity was selective. A paired history of RCA Taiwan and the separate RCA-ITRI technology transfer project shows how investment promotion and labour governance privileged officially selected industrial objectives over workers’ independent authority. Public sponsorship equipped semiconductor learning with personnel, facilities, and foreign knowledge. Labour administration, managed representation, and corporate control of hazard information restricted workers’ demands for protection. Pay, housing, and production routines made exposure difficult to avoid, while repeated inspections failed to secure compliance. Missing records, withheld information, and corporate restructuring then obstructed compensation claims. Workers and their supporters challenged these barriers by assembling legal, scientific, and archival resources. Their struggle places labour protection within the history of developmental capacity, alongside the acquisition of technology.

articles.title: Explaining historical persistence in Germany's electoral geography across 130 years: a cleavage-perspective on continuity in spatial patterns of party support
articles.abstract: This article studies the long-run persistence of electoral geographies. Drawing on cleavage theory, I argue that spatial patterns of party support persist where cleavages remain politically salient and the social groups they mobilise stay in place. I evidence this argument for Germany, combining electoral and census data from the German Empire (1890–1912) and reunified Germany (2002–2021) at the municipality, county and electoral-district level. The spatial analyses reveal substantial continuity in the electoral geographies of the mainstream left and right. The analysis traces both to one source, the persistent spatial distribution of Catholics. Christian democrats continued historical strongholds of the Center Party where Catholics stayed concentrated, while the SPD persists as its mirror image in the non-Catholic space. Persistence therefore rests on the stability of the religious geography and cleavage, not on the class cleavage and the economic geography, which has changed markedly. The findings position cleavage-based persistence as a complement to cultural-transmission accounts of historical legacies, locating continuity in the ongoing mobilisation of stable social groups rather than in transmitted attitudes alone.

articles.title: Why Politicians Retweet: News Trustworthiness, Emotion, and Partisan Asymmetry in Elite News Sharing among US Congress Members
articles.authors: Apeksha Shetty, Esther Simmendinger, Jula Lühring, Annie Waldherr, David Garcia, Hannah Metzler
articles.abstract: On social media, politicians' retweets can determine which claims gain visibility in online and in wider political debate, yet the factors associated with these retweeting decisions remain poorly understood. Combining natural language processing measures of emotional tone and partisan cues with politician-level characteristics, we analyze the retweeting behavior of United States Members of Congress between 2021 and 2023 using multilevel logistic regression models. Using all news-related retweets during this period, paired with a negative sample of non-retweets, we examine how tweet content and legislators' ideological extremity predict the amplification of tweets linking to more and less trustworthy news domains. We find that partisan identity is a stronger predictor of retweeting than other factors. While politicians generally preferred retweeting content with links to trustworthy sources, this preference weakened when tweets contained party-related references. Anger and fear predicted higher retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political opponents, while anger predicted lower retweeting likelihood when tweets referenced political allies. Furthermore, ideology conditioned how politicians responded to news trustworthiness: among Republicans, increasing ideological extremity was associated with weaker preference for trustworthy sources, with the most ideologically-extreme Republicans being especially likely to retweet tweets with links to less trustworthy domains. Together, these results suggest that politicians use retweets to reinforce partisan boundaries between 'us' and 'them'. This identity-centered pattern to retweeting explains how information from less trustworthy sources gains traction in polarized digital environments.

articles.title: When the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) is Full of Holes: The Child’s Right to Mental Health in Post-Conflict Sool and Sanaag
articles.authors: Guleid Ahmed Jama, Marieke J. Hopman
articles.abstract: This paper aims to understand the situation of children’s mental health rights in Sool and Sanaag. We apply the Children’s Rights Normative Culture (CRNC) model (Hopman et al. 2026) to a dataset of 85 research conversation conducted between May and November 2025 (40 children, 45 adults) in the two cities. A key finding from the research is that children’s mental health is not recognised as a distinct rights issue within the socio-legal orders applicable in the research area. Moreover, there is no clearly articulated or enforceable socio-legal obligation (from any socio-legal order) concerning the protection of children’s mental health. Nor do the socio-legal norms seem to establish specific remedial measures for children experiencing mental health difficulties. The language of rights is largely absent from people’s understanding of children’s mental health. Across clan, community, religious, and state normative orders, children are mainly seen through the family framework. The paper suggest that 1) children’s mental health should be seen as a children’s rights, 2) families, particularly mothers, and the community, should be engaged as key entry point for societal change, 3) space should be created for children where they can safely share their experiences and views at all levels, including the family, schools, community and post-conflict peacebuilding initiatives.

articles.title: Agreement Without Accuracy: Six Systematic Defects an LLM Annotation Study Could Not See in Its Own Reliability Statistics
articles.abstract: Researchers who use large language models as annotators are commonly asked to demonstrate reliability, and test–retest agreement under a fixed seed is the cheapest evidence. We report a study in which it was systematically misleading. Annotating 1,902 student UML class specifications under a fixed snapshot, seed and zero temperature, we compared three prompt configurations, each run twice. A three-stage pipeline appeared to raise answer-level agreement from .647 to .845, with chance-corrected agreement rising for every code and internal consistency satisfied throughout. Comparing per-code prevalence led us to inspect outputs; five systematic defects emerged: an instruction promising an input never supplied (wrong on 64.7% of its flags at κ = .971); a stage receiving element names stripped of the types it was to judge; residual error after repair; enumerated conditions firing outside their scope; and alignment tables stored without half of what they summarised. A sixth lay in our checking procedure: the audit rule we wrote agreed with a blind reading on only 67.5% of cases, and the twenty cases read to confirm it were drawn from its own output. A blind reading of forty random submissions, judged before any output was seen, is the study's only anchored estimate; under it our one reported repair cannot be shown to help. None was surfaced by a reliability statistic; those that altered the model's inputs or rules raised agreement by easing its task. Reliability from repeated runs should be accompanied by prevalence comparisons and a sample read blind, drawn independently of the detector.

articles.title: Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding
articles.abstract: In many domains, human life has undergone dramatic changes—globalized exchanges, complex technological systems, large societies—that would both require and result from rapid cognitive change. In this work, I introduce the Cultural Cognitive Scaffolding Hypothesis, which posits that (1) human cognition is uniquely culturally evolvable because our cognitive processes rely on environmental resources that are largely culturally evolvable, and, as a consequence, (2) it is these specific cultural innovations, called cultural cognitive scaffolds (CCS), that are responsible for much of the rapid, recent changes in human cognition. Importantly, to achieve this effect, these cultural innovations must balance cognitive impact and cultural success. The historical expansion of exchange networks offers an ideal case to illustrate how diverse cultural innovations helped manage the high uncertainty associated with exchanges across larger physical and cultural distances, and a window into how cultural success can be achieved for different cultural innovations. Finally, this framework has important implications for our understanding of the uniquely open-ended character of human culture.

articles.title: Identifying determinants of ecological footprints: A novel application of latent growth curve models (LGM)

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This study investigates the determinants of ecological footprint growth trajectories in 112 countries (2004–2017) using latent growth curve models (LGM). Unlike traditional panel methods, LGM captures dynamic trends and country-level heterogeneity in environmental impact over time. The approach integrates economic, institutional, and socio-geographic determinants into a unified causal framework. Results indicate that economic complexity mediates the relationship between economic growth and ecological footprint, promoting technological innovation and sustainable practices. Higher economic complexity also partially offsets environmental impacts from increased fossil fuel consumption. These findings underscore the need for policies fostering innovation, economic diversification, and sustainable urban planning to mitigate environmental degradation.

articles.title: Determinants of the relationship between growth and CO2 emissions: A novel application utilizing bivariate latent growth curve models (BLGM) across European regions

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This study investigates the key determinants shaping the dynamic relationship between economic growth and CO2 emissions in 220 European NUTS2 regions from 2000 to 2021, using a bivariate latent growth curve model (BLGM). Unlike traditional methods, the BLGM framework addresses a critical gap in modeling latent growth processes, variable interactions, and regional heterogeneity, significantly advancing previous methodologies. The approach integrates determinants of regional economic structures, energy consumption patterns, labor market characteristics, and educational attainment. The results highlight the crucial role of financial structure, spatial centrality, and educated development, offering insights for adaptive and effective regional climate and sustainability strategies and emphasizing the need for coordinated policies that integrate technological innovation, territorial planning, labor market diversification, and sustained investment in education.

articles.title: Examination of the News-Finds-Me Perception as an Expanded Bifactor Construct
articles.abstract: Within the mass and political communication literatures, the news-find-me (NFM) perception has been increasingly used to explain the democratically deleterious implications of a reliance on incidental, socially mediated news contact. Despite these efforts, there does not currently exist a consistent means of measuring the NFM construct. This study developed an expanded NFM measure and evaluated it using a latent bifactor model specification. The results suggested that a bifactor-(S·I 1) specification fit the data in a plausible manner, and, therein, that there exist research scenarios where the use of such an approach may confer benefits to researchers.

articles.title: From Affective Experience to Mechanism: A Critical Realist Case Study Architecture Using Reflexive Thematic Analysis
articles.abstract: Studying affective life qualitatively poses a known problem. Burnout, emotional labour, and slow shifts in teacher–class relations are real with measurable effects, yet not directly visible; we infer them from behaviour and language. Interpretation always mediates. How can we claim mechanisms without pretending to observe them? This paper proposes a case-study architecture using reflexive thematic analysis within a critical realist frame. It integrates five usually separate elements: a multi-perspectival case design; abduction and retroduction as genuinely different inferences; systematic assessment of rival explanations; a procedure for sorting context from mechanism when they do not separate cleanly; and a hierarchy of claims calibrated to evidence. The combination yields what neither purely interpretive nor purely causal work can: fallible mechanism explanations that take meaning and causation equally seriously. The argument is specified, not demonstrated. Two computational simulations provide proof of concept. The first distinguishes two known ground-truth mechanisms across 40 synthetic cases, with 80% overall recovery (95% CI [68%, 92%]; 85% and 75% per mechanism). The second adds a third rival—perceptual reconstruction, in which teacher behaviour is unchanged but students report change—and distinguishes all three across 60 synthetic cases, with 95% overall recovery (100%, 100%, 85%). The three-way test uses tighter noise parameters than the two-way, so rates are not directly comparable. Both test only one component and neither substitutes for empirical validation on real classroom data, which remains future work.

articles.title: Ideology on the U.S. District Courts: Reexamining Presidential and Senatorial Appointment Power
articles.authors: Nicholas O. Howard, David A Hughes, Philip Warncke
articles.abstract: Unlike U.S. appellate courts, scholars of the American federal judiciary typically lack ideological estimates for district court judges that are derived directly from their behavior. Rather, scholars have primarily relied upon proxy measures based upon the preferences of a judge's appointing president or those of home-state senators in the event senatorial courtesy is in effect. Nevertheless, senatorial courtesy is a norm, and norms can be broken. It remains an open question whether home-state senators genuinely constrain the president when it comes to the ideological tenor of appointees to the district courts. We produce novel ideal point estimates for 1,680 U.S.~district court judges appointed between 1913 and 2009 based upon their votes in approximately 100,000 cases, in addition to contextual factors unique to judges and the process by which they were appointed. We map these ideal points into the Judicial Common Space and make them publicly available to American courts scholars. These ideal points differ meaningfully compared to previous proxy measures and improve predictive power in judge voting behavior. Importantly, despite a battery of statistical tests, we find that senatorial courtesy appears to play a minimal role with respect to the revealed preferences of U.S. district court judges compared to the role the president's ideology plays. If senatorial courtesy indeed constrains presidents in the separation of powers game, it is likely on some other, non-ideological dimension.

articles.title: Staying Connected: Methodological Insights for Developing Panel Surveys with People Experiencing Homelessness
articles.authors: Caroline Teague, Aryaa Rajouria, Yuanxi Li, Brandon Morande, Hugo Aguas, Nathalie Williams, Jerald Herting, ihsan kahveci
articles.abstract: Longitudinal research on people experiencing homelessness remains rare due to challenges in sustained contact, digital access, and institutional trust. This study draws on three focus groups conducted between September 2024 and January 2025 in King County, Washington, to explore how to tailor contact modes in longitudinal surveys with persons experiencing homelessness to improve retention and reduce attrition. Participants highlighted major barriers to digital contact, including inconsistent access to phones and service, charging stations, and two-factor authentication. Email was preferred for its stability. Participants emphasized the need for transparent, scheduled communication and flexible incentives, such as Cash app. We conclude with a summary of practical suggestions to improve survey design and discuss how our findings from one particular setting can be extended more broadly around the country and world.

articles.title: The Substitution Trap: Development Aid and the Composition of Government Spending in Indian States
articles.abstract: The question of whether aid supplements or substitutes government spending has long been debated in public finance literature. Building on Vadlamannati and Iacono (2026), who examine how development aid affects discretionary fiscal transfers to Indian states, we address a distinct fiscal question: how does aid exposure affect the composition of subnational government expenditure? Using panel data for 30 Indian states over 1979-2019 (41 years) and an instrumental variable strategy addressing potential endogeneity, we find that greater exposure to aid is associated with a lower share of capital expenditure and a higher share of revenue expenditure. This pattern is consistent with substitution of externally aided projects for domestically financed spending. The effect however varies systematically with electoral incentives. In states with greater electoral competition, aid is more strongly associated with capital expenditure, suggesting that electoral incentives can encourage state governments to channel external resources towards visible capital investments. Our findings extend the evidence on fiscal consequences of aid in India from the allocation of intergovernmental discretionary transfers to the composition of state government expenditure. Our findings reveal that the developmental effects of aid depend not only on how resources reach subnational governments but also on how governments subsequently allocate them.

articles.title: Data visualization: Spanish results in PISA across waves by parental educational attainment
articles.abstract: Using Spanish PISA microdata from 2003–2025, we analyze performance trends in mathematics and reading by parental educational attainment. Results show a steady decline in scores among students from highly educated families, starting as early as 2012 in mathematics and 2015 in reading.

articles.title: Disaffording the Pedestrian: When Affordances Are Removed

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Designing for pedestrian road safety is challenging. Designs need to work for a broad and diverse range of pedestrians, while also considering the needs of other vulnerable road users, such as cyclists. Pedestrians are ranked as the most vulnerable in the road user hierarchy and designing for those with protected characteristics is critically important for road safety designers. One key challenge faced is designing the environment so that safety provisions can align with national and international goals to encourage people to walk or wheel more for health, economic and environmental reasons. Doctoral research was undertaken to understand whether and how design can improve pedestrian road safety and used key study sites in London to investigate the relationship between safety affordances in public space and pedestrian safety. One main finding was that often, during a redesign, safety features are removed. The consequences of these changes make it difficult for pedestrians to maintain their safety, particularly those with protected characteristics. Beyond potential physical harm, there are psychosocial impacts: people may avoid a route if they feel it is unsafe or leads to conflict in contested spaces which leaves pedestrians feeling unable to navigate a space confidently. These experiences are not routinely captured within road safety data, which focuses largely on KSI (killed or seriously injured) outcomes. I have coined this phenomenon of removing an affordance a disaffordance. The concept comes from over five years of doctoral research into pedestrian road safety in the UK, which focused on pedestrian-only study sites in London that had been redesigned as shared-space zones. Identifying safety affordances and disaffordances in the built environment helps to identify opportunities for broader and more systematic pedestrian participation in the design process. The research also developed GroundMap, a diagnostic approach for identifying and mapping affordances and disaffordances and anticipating the potential consequences of their removal. At a broader level, the term disaffordance might be extended to identify other environments where the removal of an affordance has significant consequences. While this research applies the concept specifically to pedestrian safety, its wider application across other environments and domains is identified here as a direction for future work.

articles.title: Monetary Policy Transmission in Nepal: A Study of How Central Bank Policy Rates Affect Bank Lending and Economic Activity
articles.abstract: Monetary policy transmission, the mechanism through which the monetary policy of the central bank impacts bank lending rates and, by extension, the broader economy, is of great interest to policymakers. This paper provides an in-depth analysis of the monetary policy transmission mechanism in the Nepalese context. It focuses on the interest rate pass-through channels and associated frictions in the Nepalese monetary policy framework. It uses the information published by NRB, the central bank of Nepal, as well as scholarly research and reports on the topic to perform the study. It highlights that the interest rate pass-through in Nepal is partial and delayed and discusses the reason why monetary policy transmissions in Nepal work as they do. The paper starts with an introduction to the topic of monetary policy transmission. Then, it proceeds to discuss research questions and objectives, theoretical background, and methodological background. Finally, it presents data analysis and discusses the findings to reach final conclusions and recommendations.

articles.title: External Debt Sustainability in Nepal: A Case Study Based on Nepal Rastra Bank, IMF, and World Bank Data
articles.abstract: External debt sustainability is a matter of great concern for many developing countries like Nepal since a part of the borrowed money is regarded as the liability that threatens to criticize the value of their local currency and increases their fiscal burden. This paper performs an analysis of the external debt indicators of Nepal and the risk of a debt distress using the information provided by Nepal Rastra Bank (NRB), International Monetary Fund (IMF) and World Bank. According to the results, the total public debt in Nepal is expected to reach about Rs 2.97 trillion (USD 19.21 billion) by the end of fiscal year 2025/26, which is equivalent to 45.07 percent of GDP, as compared to 43.79 percent in the previous year. The external debt increased to about 25.3 percent of GDP from 20.6 percent, and that of domestic one remained at about 22-23 percent. Nepal still belongs to the countries with low risk of experiencing a debt distress, according to the joint World Bank-IMF Debt Sustainability Analysis (DSA). However, the study highlights several vulnerabilities in the external debt of Nepal as the present value of the external debt-to-exports ratio exceeds the indicative threshold in the export shock scenario. The Nepali rupee has depreciated by around Rs 8 against the US dollar in the first seven months of FY2025/26, adding Rs 92.96 billion to the external debt of the country. Only around one-third of the capital budget has been spent, which implies that the borrowed money is used for sustaining the recurrent expenditure rather than capital spending. The paper concludes that Nepal’s debt is sustainable in the near term. However, the increasing vulnerabilities in the form of currency depreciation, inadequate revenue mobilization efforts and low efficiency utilization of the borrowed funds should be responded to in order to address long-term sustainability.

articles.title: Turning Ambition into Action: Lessons from the Italian National Recovery and Resilience Plan
articles.authors: Alessia Aspide, Lorenzo Mascioli, Gabriele Beretta, Camilla Locatelli
articles.abstract: The Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF) is the primary financial instrument of the EU’s ambitious pandemic response initiative, NextGenerationEU (NGEU). This report examines Italy’s capacity to implement its ambitious National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP) effectively. It opens with a comparative analysis of the NRRPs of the four largest EU economies: Germany, France, Italy, and Spain. Focusing then on Italy, the largest recipient, the report explores how state capacity shapes the implementation of ambitious reforms and investments, emphasizing the challenges of translating NGEU’s transformative goals into tangible outcomes.

articles.title: Issues and Challenges of Poverty and International Labor Migration in Nepal
articles.abstract: This paper aims to discuss the opportunity and challenges of the foreign labor market for Nepalese workers and Nepal’s government policy. The study was carried out in the form of a qualitative research method, where secondary data were used. The collected data were analyzed using the content analysis method after a close reading of the sources. This paper discussed the current situation of government policy, manpower agencies, problems of migrant workers, and the way of using the remittance. This research found that the government policy is less effective, and manpower agencies are not following the government rules and regulations. Since the last two decades, remittances have been a significant contributor to the Nepalese economy. Many scholars argued that remittance helps to reduce the country’s poverty rates. However, Nepalese workers face numerous problems in the home country and destination countries. Migrant workers are being charged high service charges and misguided by the local agent and manpower agencies in the home country Nepal. They face problems in destination countries such as low remuneration, sexual abuse, and risky job environment. Most of the remittances are using daily expenses such as purchasing foods. This paper explores these vulnerabilities of migrant workers and suggests stakeholder interventions to make safer migration and sustainably use a remittance.

articles.title: Women's Land Rights in India: A Learning Document
articles.authors: ISST, Jahnvi Andharia, Benu Verma, Saee Pawar, Ashmeet Kaur, Kritika Goel
articles.abstract: Womanity has decided to strategically accelerate gender equality and economic empowerment of women in India by developing and supporting sustainable models that look at women's land rights pathways that can be adapted and scaled across the country. The program focuses on increasing land literacy, women’s land ownership and long-term land access to secure livelihoods for 50,000 women at the community level. Womanity’s Theory of Change (ToC) Document outlines the rationale and the pathway to advance gender equality and economic empowerment of women through sustainable models and strategic interventions. Womanity has outlined three phases to reach 50,000 women – Build, Enhance and Scale. In the Build phase, it seeks to identify challenges, evolve prototype sustainable models, measure effectiveness and impact, support implements, invest in research, and develop a comprehensive evidence plan. This learning document prepared by ISST contributes to the efforts of the Build phase of Womanity. The objective of this document is to capture the learnings of the various partner organizations, key members of the Womanity team, and the other stakeholders (referred as the Womanity ecosystem in India) in the first 18 months of the project period, as well as their future learning needs. Through a thorough analysis of the data collected over six months, a learning framework was expected to map all possible needs for building knowledge and strengthening capacities within the Womanity ecosystem to effectively address various WLR issues

articles.title: Long-Term Sequences of State-Building and Violent Conflict
articles.abstract: A large body of research demonstrates that state capacity is an important correlate of intrastate conflict. However, similar levels of present-day state capacity can result from different historical trajectories of state-building. I argue that specific sequences of state-building can shape the risk of violent conflict in the long run: geographical obstacles can isolate territories from state-building processes for extended periods, strengthening non-state institutions. The risk of violence increases once the state has accumulated sufficient capabilities to close this state-building gap. The extension of authority into peripheral territories triggers resistance from among local elites that mobilize their constituencies against the central state. I exploit exogenous variation in early state-penetration in Nepal to investigate this argument. Areas located below the Himalayan foothills were heavily Malaria-infested preventing the state from establishing meaningful presence until the implementation of a malaria eradication program in the 1950/60s. I make use of this specificity in Regression Discontinuity (RD) estimations. The findings lend support to the primary arguments of the paper and underscore the role of long-term sequences of development.

articles.title: Rounding and the bill-size gradient in tipping
articles.abstract: Restaurant tip percentages often decline as bills increase. Rounding is one proposed explanation because a fixed upward adjustment adds more to the tip percentage on a small bill. We examine how much of the observed decline can be explained by adjustments of up to one dollar. We analyzed 22,446 checks with positive recorded tips, no automatic gratuity and bills of $10–$200 from three North Carolina restaurant outlets. For checks with a whole-dollar tip or reconstructed final payment, we allowed the pre-rounding tip to fall anywhere from one dollar below the recorded amount to the recorded amount, with a minimum of zero. We calculated the smallest and largest bill-size coefficients across these possible amounts, controlling for outlet, month, guest count, opening hour and weekday. Bootstrap checks resampled dates, weeks and servers. Each scheme used 999 draws, with the rounding bounds recalculated for each resampled dataset. Tip percentages fell by 4.29 points per bill doubling. Even the adjustments that most reduce this decline leave a coefficient of −1.62 points, which remains negative across all three bootstrap checks. Five-dollar rounding or restricting bills to $30–$200 allows the fitted decline to disappear. Upward dollar rounding cannot fully explain the negative gradient in the primary sample. Larger rounding increments and the exclusion of small bills produce ranges containing zero.

articles.title: Antagonistic Predictions
articles.abstract: Why do we use models to predict the most likely outcome? Integrating model predictions into high-stakes decision-making pipelines can amplify biases and introduce flawed decisions when human caseworkers and models compete over the same prediction target. Learning to anticipate the most likely outcome risks reproducing biases embedded in historical data, while delivering such predictions in human-AI decision-making raises issues of cognitive biases and algorithmic aversion versus overreliance. In this perspective, I argue for Antagonistic Predictions, a structurally different paradigm where models are tasked to act as sparring partners that challenge human pre-conceptions and show reachable futures rather than anticipating the most common pattern. I envision instantiations of Antagonistic Predictions that can counteract historical disadvantages, social stereotyping, and cognitive biases and sketch potential implementations in predictive ML and generative AI settings.

articles.title: A Geographic Accessibility Database for Health Care Services to Support Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Dementias Exposome Research
articles.authors: Amber DeJohn, Kyusik Kim, Weining Kan
articles.abstract: These datasets characterize geographic access to health care providers that are associated with modifiable risk factors for Alzheimer’s Disease and Alzheimer’s Disease-related Dementias (AD/ADRD) for the United States. We offer three measures of geographic access, including the drive time to the closest provider (i.e., nearest facility), how many providers are within a 30, 60, 90, and 120-minute drive (i.e., cumulative opportunity), and the Minimum Attainment Cost (MAC), a new measure that facilitates urban-rural comparisons at a national scale. As an intermediary data product, we provide the origin-destination matrices that are used to generate geographic access measures. We calculate geographic access scores for thirteen types of healthcare facilities at the census block group scale and provide population-weighted aggregate measures at the census tract. Researchers can use these data in tandem with demographic information and other place-based measures to characterize the reachable health care landscape in order to understand how access to care may influence modifiable risk factors for AD/ADRD.

articles.title: Sustaining Imbalance: International Financial Foundations of Growth Models
articles.authors: Benjamin Braun, Lucio Baccaro, Joshua Cova
articles.abstract: Current account imbalances, which have surged again in recent years, are key drivers of global economic instability and conflict. Political economy explanations tend to focus on wage restraint and currency undervaluation. However, in a world of unrestricted cross-border capital mobility, the binding constraint for sustaining imbalances over time is financial flows. To address this gap, we develop a theoretical framework linking current account imbalances, growth models, and domestic financialization. We hypothesize that deep and liquid financial markets enable the reproduction of consumption-led growth by relaxing the current account constraint, while financial underdevelopment favors export-led growth by incentivizing capital exports. We test our theoretical propositions with a series of error correction models and an event history analysis, based on panel data on 55 countries over the period 1970-2022. We find broad support for the theoretical expectations but a dissimilarity in the relationship between growth models and financialization: While financial development is crucial for the long-term maintenance of consumption-led growth in advanced economies especially, results are inconclusive regarding the role of financial underdevelopment as a facilitating factor for export-led growth.

articles.title: JCGE: A Modular Julia Framework for Computable General Equilibrium Modelling
articles.abstract: Computable general equilibrium (CGE) modelling requires a workflow beyond equilibrium specification and solution: data preparation, calibration, model construction, diagnostics, experiments, and results handling. JCGE is an Apache-2.0-licensed Julia framework of focused, independently versioned packages. It provides data and calibration utilities, reusable CGE blocks, a shared execution specification, diagnostics, outputs, and reference models. Application packages compose these components while retaining their own data, closures, and economic assumptions. The runtime constructs JuMP models for nonlinear and mixed-complementarity formulations without prescribing a solver. A Model Context Protocol interface supports framework discovery and owner-registered workflows. This paper presents the architecture, quality controls, and reuse potential for independently developed CGE software.

articles.title: Calling Capitalism and Class in the United States: From Reconstruction and the Gilded Age to the Present
articles.abstract: This article explains how American capitalism repeatedly transformed rather than displaced the moral language of calling. Beginning with Reconstruction and the Gilded Age, it traces how disciplined labor, self-command, thrift, and achievement were detached from Calvinist theology and reembedded in corporations, schools, professions, credit systems, welfare institutions, and digitally mediated workplaces. It develops an institutional account of moralized inequality: institutions distribute unequal resources and opportunities, then classify unequal outcomes as individual merit, responsibility, or failure. The analysis distinguishes property, organizational authority, expertise, income, wealth, employment security, debt exposure, and institutional dependence, while showing how race, gender, citizenship, education, occupation, and locality convert historically unequal resources into apparently individual merit. Calling persists as a contested moral infrastructure of capitalism. The central question is whether institutions that demand effort, commitment, and self-investment can justify the unequal security, authority, wealth, and recognition that follow.

articles.title: Dignity Defense Model : A Study on the Structural Mismatch in Employment of Female University Students in China and Its Shaping Mechanism on the Decline in Fertility Rate
articles.abstract: Millions of female university graduates in China face a severe shortage of standardized office jobs with weekends off each year. This structural mismatch exacerbates employment pressure. Drawing on empirical data from the Anhui provincial civil service examination, this paper proposes a “dignity-defense-oriented reproductive decision-making model.” Confronted with the gap between high career expectations and labor-market reality, female university students, motivated by dignity defense and risk aversion toward the motherhood penalty, prefer survival strategies such as “slow employment” and the “civil service examination craze” over marriage and childbearing. These choices significantly suppress the overall birth rate. To address this dilemma, the paper recommends reconstructing the university employment-quality evaluation system and disciplinary structure, introducing national policies that reduce the motherhood penalty, and promoting a shift in the macro-market toward consumption infrastructure centered on independent women.

articles.title: An Assessment of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report on Sociology
articles.abstract: The Sociology portion of the Vanderbilt-Washington University Report (VWUR) claims to have studied the discipline of sociology and asserts that sociology’s search for truth has been compromised by what the author calls “politicization.” I find that the VWUR’s claims are unsubstantiated and based upon fundamental errors. The problem is not lack of data but rather that the author, Dr. Ashley Rubin, misunderstands and misrepresents the data she does have while failing to check her own biases. She mistakenly reads politicization into everything she sees, reaffirming a thesis she had already held before her supposedly impartial study without taking the appropriate steps to suspend her bias. The VWUR violates the very social scientific standards that it purports to defend while distracting us from other problems facing social science.

articles.title: What the World Studies, Invents and Reports About Urban Heat
articles.abstract: We assemble 20,422 scholarly papers on urban heat islands (1990–2025), read the 17,101 that carry an abstract sentence by sentence, and join them to 96,726 news articles (2021–2025), 4,123 patent families, 14,576 recorded heat incidents, registers of companies, funding rounds and government funding events, and the annual accounts of Indian companies. Eight results stand out. (1) The field grew about 9 times faster than the scholarly literature as a whole, and in 2015–2019 titles naming "extreme heat" overtook those naming "heat island". (2) Of 2,409 papers that attribute urban heat to a cause, 48% name urbanisation and land-use change; attribution to anthropogenic heat fell from 18.4% to 7.7%. (3) Research and news describe different problems: at equal text length, 28% of research openings raise mitigation against 1.6% of news leads, while 22% of news leads are forecasts or warnings against 1.4% of research. (4) They also describe different places: China accounts for 31% of the research and 2.3% of English-language coverage, and Delhi receives 7.4 times the coverage its research share would predict. (5) Invention has outrun science: patent families for cool and permeable pavements grew 12-fold in a decade against 2.4-fold for the research on them. (6) Across 194 studies the median reported cooling from urban trees is 2.0 °C (air temperature 2.0 °C, surface temperature 2.9 °C). (7) Between 2021–22 and 2024–25 news coverage moved from the hazard to the people exposed: workers, schools, the elderly and hospital patients each rose 1.4- to 2.4-fold as a share of heat articles while wildfire and drought fell by about half and climate change — raised in about one article in ten — fell by a quarter. (8) The market record is thin: 140 of 5.05 million companies state a heat or cooling purpose, and recorded capital is $2.7 billion of cooling-infrastructure finance against $48 million of venture funding; larger Indian cooling companies grew revenue 25% a year over three years against 16% for Indian companies generally. Every cause category extracted from the research was tested against an independent second reader; three failed, and no result reported here rests on them.

articles.title: Financial Sector Stability and Credit Growth in Nepal: A Case Study
articles.abstract: Nepal’s financial system has undergone waves of credit booms, especially in the pre- and post-COVID-19 pandemic periods, which raises questions about the health of the banking sector. This paper examines the association between credit growth and banking sector health using secondary data from Nepal Rastra Bank and the International Monetary Fund. The World Bank for fiscal years 2016/17-2023/24. It is found that private sector credit grew at nearly 29 percent in 2016/17 and more than 27 percent in 2020/21, which far exceeded the overall economy’s growth rates. Credit boomed due to large remittance inflows, low real interest rates, and rapid expansion of bank outlets and digital products. Heavy lending to real estate, housing, construction, and import sectors. Consequently, the quality of banks’ assets declined as credit growth slowed down sharply in 2021/22. The non-performing loan ratio, which averaged between 1.2 and 1.8 percent during the boom years, rose to about 2.6 percent in 2022/23 and 3.7 percent in 2023/24. The capital adequacy ratio of banks dipped from 14.5 percent in 2016/17 to 12.8 percent in 2023/24. The study concludes that rapid credit growth, albeit beneficial for a short time, may pose significant financial stability risks if the lending environment worsens and credit becomes concentrated in a few sectors. The paper recommends enhanced risk-based supervision, countercyclical capital buffers, diversification of credit to productive sectors, improved governance, and enhanced capital markets to complement bank lending

articles.title: Social Ecology and Diagnostic Visibility: A Cross-National Analysis of Autism Spectrum Disorder Prevalence in 55 Countries
articles.abstract: Cross-national variation in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) prevalence is commonly attributed to differences in diagnostic infrastructure and case ascertainment. We tested whether cultural individualism predicts this variation independently of detection capacity, and whether the result is robust to known limitations of Hofstede's widely used but methodologically dated Individualism Index (IDV). Using 55 countries (GBD 2019 ASD prevalence, World Bank GDP, an author-constructed diagnostic infrastructure index, Hofstede's IDV, and a recently validated individualism-collectivism index built from nationally representative survey data; Akaliyski et al., 2025), we found the raw individualism-ASD correlation is robust to measurement choice (Hofstede: r = 0.702; validated index: r = 0.624; both p < .001, n = 47 non-screening countries with both measures available). However, its apparent independence from detection capacity is not robust: partial correlations controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure remain significant with Hofstede's IDV (partial r = 0.30-0.39) but collapse to non-significance with the validated index (partial r = -0.14 to 0.09, ns), because the validated index correlates far more strongly with diagnostic infrastructure (r = 0.919) than Hofstede's IDV does (r = 0.818). The four mandatory-screening countries (Japan, South Korea, Singapore, Taiwan) exceed their IDV-predicted prevalence under both measures, though less dramatically using the validated index (1.57x vs. 2.84x), indicating measurement error in Hofstede's scores inflated the original screening-policy estimate. These findings show the bivariate cultural-prevalence association is genuine, but caution against treating it as evidence independent of detection capacity without testing robustness to cultural measurement choice.

articles.title: Using Hierarchical Models to Estimate Heterogeneous Effects
articles.abstract: Conditional theories are ubiquitous in political science, but standard interaction models cannot handle this proliferation of theoretically informed modifiers. This paper describes why, when, and how to use hierarchical models to encompass multiple sources of heterogeneity and regularize estimates. Doing so is simple, and starts with identifying the key sources of heterogeneity and grouping observations accordingly. Next, fit a hierarchical model with two linked regressions, one connecting treatment with the outcome, and another that models the treatment effects with potential sources of heterogeneity and partially pools group estimates. This captures systematic and random variation in heterogeneous effects, encompasses many interactions, and fits commonly used modeling frameworks, but regularization in this model breaks down if there are many small groups. I document these claims with a simulation analysis and reanalysis of a published study.

articles.title: Theravada Buddhism in Contemporary China and Its Followers
articles.abstract: This paper studies the influence of Theravada Buddhism in contemporary China, with a focus on the seven ethnic minorities that share a considerable presence of Theravada Buddhism. It also considers the populations of Theravada Buddhists among the seven ethnic minorities, as well as from another 49 official-recognized ethnicities. It discovers that the Theravada Buddhist population increases from 1.3868 million in 2010 to 1.4519 million in 2018 and is expected to grow to 1.4786 million by 2027. The present study finds that the Dai ethnicity is not only essential for spreading Theravada Buddhism to other ethnicities but it also has the largest Theravada Buddhist ethnicity in China, which represents more than 72% of the total Theravada Buddhist population. Finally, it discloses that the seven ethnicities each have their own forms of folk religions with their faith showing a mix of folk religion with Theravada Buddhism.

articles.title: The Dai People and Their Relationship with Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan: A Profile and Population Analysis
articles.abstract: Focusing on the Dai people of Yunnan, China, this study explores their demographics and Theravada Buddhist practices, examining their influence on neighboring ethnicities. It investigates how Theravada Buddhist temples serve as cornerstones of cultural identity and community cohesion, offering novel insights into the trajectory of Theravada Buddhism within Dai communities. The study employs two innovative approaches to estimate the Theravada Buddhist population in Yunnan and China. Firstly, it leverages data from the Pew Foundation survey conducted in neighboring countries. Secondly, it analyzes temple density in Xishuangbanna and Dehong. Both approaches converge on a figure of roughly 1.1 million Theravada Buddhists residing in Yunnan in 2016. Furthermore, the study estimates the total Theravada Buddhist population in Mainland China to be approximately 1.14 million in 2015 and 1.16 million in 2020. Significantly, the research reveals that the dominance of the Dai people within Theravada Buddhist communities comprised 87.7% of Theravada Buddhists in Yunnan. These findings shed light on the interplay among religious affiliation, temple density, and demographic profile, providing the religious landscape in Dai- dominated regions.

articles.title: Going Beyond the Method of Description from a Critical Realist View
articles.abstract: This paper draws on Margaret Archer's Morphogenetic Framework in a postcolonial political-economic context to examine narrative and biographical interviews from migrant households in a place named Kaliyaganj, West Bengal, in eastern India. It addresses a central methodological challenge in Critical Realism, which is regarding the move from narrative accounts of lived experience to the explanation of underlying causal mechanisms. To operationalise this, I have developed a process-based heuristic, the Trigger–Pathway–Feedback (TPF) process, which allowed me to sensitise the processual framework, followed by two more systematic analyses, which enable tracing disruption and reinforcement across migrant trajectories. By analysing recurring patterns, the study shows that migration instability is not a series of isolated events but a processual outcome of interacting structural constraints and reflexive adjustments. This gives rise to the concept of Reflexivity Traps and the formation of a conceptual subject figure, Flux Migrants.

articles.title: Evidence and Overreach in the Rubin and Commission Reports
articles.abstract: The report on “The Status of Scholarly Standards in Sociology,” authored by Dr. Ashley Rubin, claims that sociology has been “compromised” by “politicization.” In particular, it claims that “institutionalized political commitments now influence the field’s norms, priorities, and evaluation of scholarship” (pg. 5) to such an extent that “we can no longer call sociology, as a field, a data-driven social science of society” (pg. 107). I agree that some of the phenomena Rubin identifies warrant concern and deserve serious consideration and reflection. However, my assessment of the report concludes that its broad diagnosis far outruns the proffered evidence.

articles.title: Agreeing in Principle, Disagreeing on Policy: How Beliefs About the Gender Pay Gap Shape Fairness Concerns and Policy Preferences
articles.authors: Fabian Kalleitner, Jule	Adriaans, Ole Brüggemann, Cristóbal Moya, Sandra Bohmann
articles.abstract: Willingness to reduce gender inequalities partly depends on whether people are aware of them and consider them unfair. Extending scholarship centered on inequality misperceptions, we focus on beliefs about the sources of the gender pay gap (GPG), experimentally varying people's ability to attribute pay disparities to women's choices. Preregistered survey experiments in the U.S. and Germany show that information about larger (vs. smaller) and within-job (vs. overall) GPGs independently increases awareness, raises perceived unfairness, and translates into general support for government action. Initially less-supportive groups (conservatives, men) showed some of the largest increases in general support. Yet, updated beliefs did not increase support for specific policies, such as pay transparency laws or gender quotas. These findings suggest that information campaigns can affect beliefs about GPG's size and sources, but even perceiving GPGs as unfair does not bridge the gap between abstract commitment to gender equality and concrete policy support.

articles.title: Migration–Citizenship Trajectories and Institutional Incorporation: Long-Term Mental Health Consequences
articles.abstract: Migration does not necessarily produce equivalent changes in institutional membership. This study examines how geographical mobility and institutional citizenship unfold jointly across adulthood and whether differentiated pathways of institutional incorporation are associated with long-term mental health. We analysed longitudinal data from 8,297 adults aged 60–80 in the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study (CHARLS, 2011–2020). Sequence analysis reconstructed joint trajectories of rural–urban residence and institutional citizenship (hukou) between ages 15 and 60, which were linked to depressive symptoms (CES-D-10) using multilevel growth-curve models. Substantial inequalities emerged across migration–citizenship trajectories and persisted throughout later life. Rural–urban migrant workers retaining rural hukou, historically associated with more restricted access to urban social rights and protection, had depressive-symptom levels comparable to lifelong rural residents, whereas trajectories involving urban hukou were associated with more favourable outcomes. Longer migration duration was associated with modestly lower depressive symptoms among women, while the estimated association was essentially flat among men. The findings demonstrate that geographical mobility does not necessarily entail institutional incorporation and that the long-term consequences of migration depend on how geographical and institutional mobility are configured across adulthood.

articles.title: Personal Reflections on Social Anthropology: A Matter of Survival
articles.abstract: One's private space (both domestic and personal) is an unarguable place of ''culture'' in the multiple meanings such word encloses. Thus, privacy is the quintessential place of practices, habits, and routines; material and immaterial transit and acquisition; production and reproduction; relationships, affections, and memories. Only due to having it ''too close'', could its highly valuable ethnographic density go unnoticed. In this work, the author shares some learnings acquired during his very intense life in the form of a tale. The action is placed in his kitchen, where he imagines out loud how precious it would be to gather all his memories there at the present time.

articles.title: Assessing and identifying special protection needs among refugees in the EU: Overview and Synthesis of Evidence and Policy Recommendations
articles.authors: Niklas Nutsch, Maren Hintermeier, Andreas W. Gold, Clara Perplies, Nils Robson, Veronika Wiemker, Till Bärnighausen, Sven Rohleder, Kayvan Bozorgmehr

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: The EU’s Reception Conditions Directive requests member states to identify special protection needs among asylum seekers and refugees, but assessment practices remain inconsistently implemented across Europe. We systemically searched scientific and grey literature and synthesised evidence of 81 eligible documents to identify recommendations for assessing special protection needs and their implications for policy and practice. The evidence indicates that vulnerability, which may necessitate special protection, is multidimensional, intersectional, and dynamic. This requires early, continuous, and multimethod assessment rather than one-off screening. Effective assessment systems combine standardised procedures with individualised assessment, referral pathways, and multidisciplinary collaboration. We identified 51 screening tools, however, no single tool was universally accepted and used, highlighting that implementation depends less on individual tools than on coordinated, person-centred systems supported by rights-based documentation, informed consent, and secure information sharing. These findings provide evidence-informed directions for strengthening assessment of special protection needs systems across the EU.

articles.title: Provisioning for human needs at low resource use: institutional lessons from Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador
articles.authors: Chirag Dhara, Gustav Cederlöf, Viviana Cordero, Carolina Mauri, Tannya Pico, Soumyajit Bhar
articles.abstract: In the pursuit of sustainable development, Global South countries face the challenge of advancing wellbeing without breaching environmental limits. A central question for development policy is what institutional and policy configurations can deliver high levels of human need satisfaction at low ecological cost. We address this through structured comparative case studies of Cuba, Costa Rica and Ecuador: three middle-income countries achieving health and educational outcomes comparable to higher-income nations with considerably lower environmental impacts, while also differing widely on the political-economic spectrum. Situating them within a social provisioning framework, we analyse the exogenous endowments, external conditions, structural-institutional configurations and concrete policies that account for their performance. Five cross-cutting patterns emerge across otherwise divergent political contexts: 1. sustained public investment in health and education, protected from fiscal volatility even during economic crises has been the foundational mechanism of needs satisfaction among all three; 2. periods of institutional stability have been preconditions for transformative legislation; 3. land tenure reform and food system restructuring have functioned simultaneously as instruments of ecological governance and social equity; 4. organised civil society has proved facilitative for sustaining provisioning gains across political transitions, although in Cuba such organisation has occurred within the politicised framework of the state; and 5. low energy and material throughput has been induced at least partly by resource constraint rather than by design. For the Global South, these cases offer a spectrum of configurations that can enable the satisfaction of human needs at moderate levels of affluence.

articles.title: Living Arrangements, Going Outdoors, and Well-Being Among Older Persons: Examining Their Associations in a Swedish Population
articles.authors: Jeanette Melin, Marie-Louise Möllerberg, Marit Preuter, Kristofer Årestedt
articles.abstract: Aim: This study examined associations between living arrangement, frequency of going outdoors, and well-being among older persons in Sweden, with particular attention to their interaction. Methods: Community-dwelling older persons (n = 1,727) across nine Swedish municipalities participated in a cross-sectional survey. Well-being was assessed using the Older Persons’ Well-being Scale (OPWELLS). Linear regression models examined associations and interactions. Results: Living alone was associated with lower well-being compared to cohabiting, whereas going outdoors more frequently was associated with higher well-being. The association between living arrangement and well-being differed by outdoor frequency. Conclusions: Frequency of going outdoors was strongly associated with well-being irrespective of living arrangement. However, the association between living alone and well-being varied with outdoor frequency. Thus, living alone should not be considered an isolated indicator of lower well-being in older age and highlights the importance of considering living arrangements within the broader context of older persons’ everyday lives.

articles.title: Orange Cones and Urban Stress: A Population-Based Survey of 1,033 Residents in Greater Montreal
articles.authors: Emmanuel Stip, Marie Claude Delisle, Shekinah Martino, Charles-Édouard Giguère, Jean Caron
articles.abstract: Abstract Background: Urban environments expose residents to recurrent low-intensity stressors, including traffic congestion, construction activity, noise, visual overload, disrupted mobility, and unpredictability. In Montreal, orange traffic cones have become an unusually prominent feature of the streetscape and a symbol of construction-related urban disruption. The terms “Montreal syndrome” and “conophobia” were previously proposed as heuristic concepts to explore the psychological significance of this phenomenon. Population-level data, however, have been lacking. Objective: To examine the frequency of exposure to orange traffic cones among residents of Greater Montreal and characterize associated behavioural responses, emotional reactions, perceived effects on quality of life, and perceptions of their relevance to mental health and well-being. Methods: A cross-sectional population survey was conducted in collaboration with an independent professional polling company using a general-population panel. A total of 1,033 adults completed a structured questionnaire assessing exposure to orange traffic cones and heavily marked construction zones, behavioural adaptation, emotional reactions, perceived impact on quality of life, and perceived relevance to mental health and well-being. Associations with sociodemographic characteristics were examined using Pearson chi-square tests. Results: The most unexpected finding concerned perceived mental-health relevance: 56.1% of respondents considered the phenomenon, at least to some extent, a potential mental-health or well-being issue (16.0% “yes, definitely” and 40.1% “yes, to some extent”). Orange-cone exposure was frequent, with 44.1% noticing cones daily or several times per day, and 76.9% reported modifying their behaviour often or sometimes because of cones or heavily marked construction zones. On the multiple-response item, 51.4% of respondents selected slowing down as a precaution, 31.0% changing route or avoiding the area, 27.2% irritation, and 12.3% anxiety or worry. Overall, 67.6% rated the impact on quality of life at the midpoint or higher on a five-point scale. Several sociodemographic associations were observed, particularly for age, employment status, and parental status. Conclusions: Repeated exposure to orange traffic cones and construction-related disruption is associated with measurable behavioural responses and perceived effects on quality of life in a substantial proportion of Greater Montreal residents. Particularly striking was that more than half of respondents themselves attributed potential mental-health or well-being relevance to the phenomenon. The findings do not establish conophobia as a discrete psychiatric disorder, but provide preliminary population-level support for a measurable dimensional construct of urban environmental stress, ranging from normal adaptation to potentially clinically significant distress.

articles.title: Envisioning transition pathways for a sustainable meat and protein supply system in Japan: A Research through Design approach
articles.authors: Maoko Fujisaki, Shiori Fujimaki, Taro Mochizuki, Naoki Mashimo, Kenichi Taki, Kenji Takasaki, Miki Saijo, Yuki Taoka, Momoko Nakatani, Takumi Ohashi
articles.abstract: The transition toward sustainable protein supply is constrained by consumer, supply-side, and policy barriers that are often studied separately, leaving unclear how a cross-domain lock-in diagnosis can inform multilevel intervention pathways. In Japan, small, dispersed farmland and imported-feed dependence intersect with established expectations of price and convenience. This exploratory case study examined Japan’s meat and protein supply system through a Research through Design approach integrating the multi-level perspective and Transition Design. Interviews with 21 participants and a co-creation workshop were used to structure current problems, envision desirable futures, and backcast potential interventions. The diagnosis showed how regulative, normative, and cognitive rules mutually reinforce these structural and cultural constraints. The research team synthesized participant outputs into three contrasting scenarios: pasture-raised lean beef, localized circular communities, and food-printer technology. Cross-scenario comparison yielded two provisional design principles: creating experiential proximity, which makes unfamiliar transition options tangible through situated experience, and culturally situated value translation, which connects sustainability values with meanings embedded in existing food cultures. The principles were instantiated differently and combined with pathway-specific system and governance components, including grading standards and sales channels, interorganizational coordination, and food law, labeling, and safety standards. The contribution lies in translating fragmented actor perspectives and a cross-domain lock-in diagnosis into a future-oriented intervention portfolio while making the interpretive steps traceable. The resulting principles and configurations provide testable propositions for comparative research and future pilot studies.

articles.title: Causal Inference in the CLS Cohort Studies
articles.authors: Liam Wright, Georgia D Tomova, Martin N. Danka, George Ploubidis, Richard J. Silverwood
articles.abstract: Correlations between variables in cohort and other observational studies do not necessarily indicate causal effects and may instead reflect bias due to confounding, sample selection processes, or measurement issues. Thankfully, multiple statistical methods, frameworks, and research designs have been developed that – when used judiciously – can aid making causal inferences with observational data. This is especially the case with CLS’s cohorts, which have several properties (e.g., longitudinal assessment and rich and varied data collection) that that can make the assumptions of these methods more plausible or provide ample opportunities for each method’s use. In this guide, we provide an overview of the possibilities for causal inference in CLS’s cohorts. Specifically, we: (1) provide background on the problem of causal inference in observational data, (2) detail the attributes of CLS’s cohorts that can support causal inference, and (3) outline an extensive set of methods and research designs that – assumptions permitting – can be used to estimate causal effects in CLS’s cohort data, illustrating each with existing applications and highlighting opportunities for further work.

articles.title: Detecting Inequality in Noisy Communication: Promises and Pitfalls of Large Language Models
articles.authors: Susanne Reinhardt, Jonathan J.B. Mijs, David	Schieferdecker, Michael Vaughan
articles.abstract: How inequality is communicated shapes how it is explained, understood, and legitimated or contested. Yet studying these communicative processes at scale is challenging because inequality is multidimensional, often expressed implicitly and relationally, and context dependent. We argue that large language models (LLMs) shift, but do not eliminate, these methodological challenges. We trace the development from manual content analysis to rule-based computational approaches and machine learning to LLMs and assess how these methods combine conceptual alignment, semantic sensitivity, contextual sensitivity, and scalability. LLMs help relax some longstanding trade-offs between semantic sensitivity to meaning and scalability, thus promising more comprehensive analyses of established research questions and opening possibilities for comparative research across contexts. Yet untapping their full potential for research on inequality communication depends on addressing problems concerning conceptual validity, representation, comparative measurement, and substantive inference. We conclude by outlining a research agenda for rigorous LLM-based inequality communication research.

articles.title: An Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK: a fine-grained typology of economic activities from open, large-scale web archive data
articles.authors: Leonardo Castro Gonzalez, Emmanouil Tranos, Levi Wolf, Rui Zhu, Emerald Dilworth
articles.abstract: We present the Atlas of Economic Activities in the UK, a granular and dynamic typology of economic activities. Built using large-scale web data from Common Crawl, the Atlas captures how UK businesses describe their economic activities, creates an activity typology and geolocates them at the postcode level. The Atlas provides a complementary source to established industrial classifications, which are static and insensitive to the evolution of economic activities. It is designed to support research and policy analysis requiring fine-grained information about economic activities over space and time. The Atlas is developed transparently using open tools and web archive data, so that it can be replicated and adapted to different research and policy contexts.

articles.title: What is edtech for? A cross-national popularity index of educational apps
articles.abstract: Digitalisation in education is so far described through broad indicators such as market growth, venture capital investment, infrastructure provision, or device availability in schools and homes. While useful, these measures reveal little about for what purposes digital technologies are used in education, and how these purposes vary across national contexts and time. This article addresses these gaps by developing an education app popularity index based on daily top-200 education app rankings across twelve countries between 2017 and 2023: Belgium, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Norway, Poland, Spain, Switzerland, the United Kingdom, and the United States. Drawing on app metadata, education apps are categorised according to the services and functions they offer to understand for what purpose they serve. The ranking is then aggregated to analyse category prominence over time and across countries to understand popularity of education apps by category. The study makes three contributions. First, it provides a granular account of what educational apps offer, showing that the educational app landscape is not dominated by a single type of service but consists of a heterogeneous mixture of tutoring tools, management platforms, parent-facing communication apps and a range of apps supporting infomal learning. Second, it shows the popularity of different types of digital education services and how and their popularity shift over time. Third, it shows that these patterns vary across country contexts. Differences across countries point to that edtech usage is not only driven by individual preferences but by distinct institutional arrangements and cultures. Lastly, this study also advances a methodological approach for understanding the realities of edtech deployment by using Google Play Store data, the world’s largest app market in terms of content volume.

articles.title: The Vanishing Mutual Citation
articles.abstract: Mutual citation – a pair of publications that cite each other – provides a simple measure of reciprocation linkage within scientific literature. Such pairs arise because papers are not published in strict sequence: authors often cite each other's preprints and working papers, add citations during revision, and sometimes publish related papers together. Using OpenAlex citation data from 1975 to 2023, we ask two questions: how has the rate at which papers reciprocate citations changed over five decades, and are interdisciplinary papers reciprocated less often than non-interdisciplinary papers? Contrary to both expectations, reciprocation declined sharply rather than rising with improved discoverability of scholarly work, and interdisciplinary papers did not reciprocate less than non-interdisciplinary papers. Mean mutual citations per paper fell by ~88% and the pooled mutual-citation rate fell by ~95% between 1975 and 2023. Papers citing three or more fields (interdisciplinary) exceeded the reciprocation rates of papers citing one or two fields (non-interdisciplinary) across a central band of six reference-count deciles (10-46 references, accounting for approximately 58% of the corpus), reciprocating up to 17% more. The two groups converged at 47-64 references (a 0.6% gap, non-interdisciplinary papers slightly ahead), and non-interdisciplinary papers reciprocated up to 28% more at the shortest and longest reference lists (3-9 and 65-5,000 references).

articles.title: Researcher well-being as a leading indicator in research-funding governance: A system dynamics exploration of top-down versus bottom-up allocation

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Governments face a recurring dilemma in dividing public research funding between top-down, competitive, mission-oriented programmes and bottom-up, investigator-led institutional grants. This research note presents an exploratory system dynamics model that endogenizes researcher motivation, conceived following self-determination theory as a slow-moving stock of psychological capital, within the feedback structure linking funding allocation, research outputs, and societal returns. Simulation experiments across three policy scenarios reveal a consistent time-asymmetric pattern. First, accelerating the shift toward competitive funding produces an earlier but lower peak in societal returns, followed by sustained decline. Second, shifting toward bottom-up funding restores motivation but opens a transition valley in returns whose depth grows with transition speed. Third, delayed corrective reallocation exhibits hysteresis: once motivation is depleted, even aggressive reallocation requires roughly two decades before returns recover. One-at-a-time sensitivity analysis indicates that these qualitative patterns persist across the tested parameter ranges, while the level of long-run returns proves highly sensitive to the weight placed on discretionary research time, around which the baseline system undergoes a regime shift. The model implies that researcher well-being functions as a leading indicator of research-system health, preceding declines in publication-based lagging indicators. We derive three testable propositions and outline an agenda for empirical calibration, beginning with a national baseline survey of researchers being launched in Japan. For funding governance, the results imply that monitoring leading indicators and pacing allocation transitions matter as much as choosing the allocation ratio itself.

articles.title: Reassessing the Role of Offline Teachers in the Era of Online Learning: In the context of India’s National Education Policy 2020
articles.abstract: India’s National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 envisages a substantial expansion of higher education and identifies online education as an important instrument for increasing access. The assumption that online learning can simultaneously expand educational access and reduce instructional costs, however, requires closer examination, particularly when online courses are incorporated into regular undergraduate and postgraduate programmes. This paper examines whether such integration can sustain the completion rates and learning outcomes normally expected from regular classroom-based education. Drawing on reported completion-to-registration data from selected online education providers, a critical review of the literature on learner engagement and learning outcomes, and a conceptual analysis of different pedagogical approaches, the study examines the relationship between learner maturity, self-directed learning, teacher interaction, and instructional requirements. The analysis suggests that large-scale access to online content does not necessarily translate into comparable levels of course completion. It further argues that pedagogical approaches designed to enhance engagement—including blended learning, active learning, problem-based learning, and personalised instruction—require sustained interaction with teachers, mentors, or facilitators. The paper therefore questions the assumption that online education will necessarily reduce instructional requirements. It proposes a hybrid pedagogical model in which online learning complements rather than replaces classroom teaching for young learners, supported by structured facilitation and mentorship to sustain completion rates and learning outcomes. Despite their low completion rates, fully online courses may be particularly appropriate for mature, self-directed lifelong learners seeking flexible opportunities for continuous skill and knowledge development.

articles.title: Beyond Marginal Fidelity: An Estimand-Matched Audit of LLM-Simulated Chinese Public Opinion
articles.abstract: Validation of LLM-generated “silicon samples” has progressed from marginal distributions to multivariate structure, but aggregate diagnostics do not establish whether the estimands on which social-scientific conclusions depend are preserved.
