Our estimand-matched audit asks whether the same demographic regression fitted to human and silicon responses from identical Chinese General Social Survey (CGSS) personas yields the same coefficient-level conclusions. We evaluate four 2026 models, two US-developed and two China-developed, at N = 1,000 per model and wave on two independent CGSS waves (2017 and 2021). Cross-wave claims rest on the 10 matched items with person-level responses in both waves. The model with the best marginal fit still showed target-coefficient discrepancies in both 2017 and 2021. All four models produced a positive pooled income association in each wave, although the matched human benchmark was close to zero. The displacement was concentrated in the perceived-fairness and general-trust items. Three models reversed the urban–rural association, and the point estimates of the sex-related distortion changed direction between waves. Serving-route differences reversed one model’s marginal-fidelity ranking. Distributional fit does not ensure that the coefficients a downstream analysis would report are preserved. Validation must target the estimand itself.

articles.title: Loneliness in the Brain: Distinguishing Between Hypersensitivity and Hyperalertness
articles.authors: Joe Bathelt, Corine Dijk, Marte Otten
articles.abstract: Introduction: Loneliness has emerged as a pressing public health issue, necessitating greater understanding of its mechanisms to devise effective treatments. While the link between loneliness and biased social cognition is a commonly proposed, the precise nature of this relationship remains unclear. This study aims to investigate the cognitive processes underlying loneliness, specifically distinguishing between hypersensitivity (heightened initial response) and hyperalertness (slow habituation) to social stimuli in lonely individuals. Methods: In Study 1, 36 participants were tested to identify the relevant EEG channels and time windows that show differential processing of angry vs happy faces and first vs later exposure in a roving oddball paradigm. Study 2 will compare these face processing effects in lonely and non-lonely participants. We aim to recruit a sample of 50 lonely and 50 non-lonely participants, who will be identified by their responses on a standardised loneliness questionnaire with population norms. Results: In Study 1, a greater response to angry compared to happy facial expressions was observed between 120-170ms over posterior and central channels, and between 360 and 470ms over right posterior channels. A greater response to the initial compared to the fifth presentation of an emotional face was found between 480 and 600ms over right posterior and central channels. These findings align with previous research on emotion and novelty processing in similar experiments. For Study 2, we anticipate observing higher response amplitudes when comparing angry expressions to happy expressions in lonely participants, indicating hypersensitivity. Furthermore, we expect to see greater amplitudes when comparing early presentations to late presentations of angry faces in lonely individuals, indicating increased alertness. Discussion: to be added at Stage 2

articles.title: Empirical Reasoning About FOI Request Delays in the European Union
articles.abstract: Freedom of information (FOI) is a human right and an important concept for the transparency and accountability of governments and public administrations. It is also essential for democracy. Despite a long research lineage on FOI laws and their use by citizens, existing empirical knowledge is still limited regarding the inner workings of FOI requests. This limitation applies particularly to the European Union (EU) and the documents possessed by its various institutions. To help at addressing this limitation, the paper presents a few empirical observations about FOI requests in the EU context. By using a dataset containing 500 requests made between 2022 and early 2023, the insight presented cover the EU institutions targeted, the requesters making FOI requests, and particularly the bureaucratic delays in handling of FOI requests. According to results based on a regression analysis, the bureaucratic delays vary according to both the EU institutions and the individual requesters.

articles.title: Responsibility to Prepare: From Individual Security to Collective Resilience
articles.authors: Paulus Damgaard, Jonas Toubøl, Lærke Høgenhaven

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: In the context of heightened geopolitical tensions, European societies increasingly frame private crisis preparedness as integral to societal resilience. Once viewed as antisocial survivalists, preppers now offer insight into civil society’s role in prepar-edness. Drawing on a netnographic study of one of Denmark’s largest Facebook prepper groups (2015-2024), this article examines how the group members per-ceive responsibility for crisis preparedness across four periods: before COVID-19, during the pandemic, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and following the Danish government’s 2024 appeal for household preparedness. Findings reveal a dominant individualistic framing in stable times, but a shift towards collective understandings of responsibility following official communication during crises. The article con-tributes to sociological research on crisis preparedness by demonstrating how per-ceptions of crisis contexts and state communication shape preppers’ responsibility frames, challenging static portrayals of preppers as antisocial and highlighting how individualised practices of preparedness can evolve into collective orientations that complement state capacity.

articles.title: Your AI Knows Your Story. Should It Die With You?
articles.abstract: Personal conversations with AI assistants increasingly contain memories, reflections, and records of changing judgment that may outlive their users. This commentary argues that selected exchanges could form a digital legacy: not a posthumous replica, but a personal testimony curated while the person is still able to correct it. Such legacies may be especially meaningful for people who wish to pass on their experience beyond their immediate family. Their creation, however, requires explicit consent, designated recipients, durable access, and a clear separation between the user's own words, the system's contributions, and any interpretations generated later. Whether such archives transmit wisdom or support bereavement remains an open question.

articles.title: Social Networks and Unequal Income Returns to Education: Gender Differences and Cross-National Context
articles.authors: INVEST Flagship, Emmi Mäkeläinen, Aki Koivula
articles.abstract: This study examines how social networks are associated with unequal income returns to education and whether these associations vary by gender and across national contexts. Using data from the International Social Survey Programme (ISSP) 2017 from representative samples in 15 countries, the study analyses the interrelations between educational attainment, social ties, and personal income. The analyses distinguish both the status of social contacts and the type of ties to the upper middle class, while also examining variation by gender and country-level income inequality. The results show that access to upper-middle-class contacts is associated with wider educational differences in income, and that close ties, especially family members, relatives, and close friends, are more strongly associated with income than weaker ties. These patterns also vary by gender, with educated men’s income more strongly associated with upper-middle-class ties than educated women’s. In addition, educational differences in the association between social networks and income are more pronounced in countries with higher levels of income inequality. The study contributes to research on social stratification by showing that income returns to education are socially embedded and also vary by gender and national context.

articles.title: The Electoral Costs of Exclusion: Women’s Candidate Placement and Party Performance
articles.abstract: Political elites continue to behave as if including women in electable positions is electorally risky, despite growing evidence of voter support for gender-inclusive representation. This paper advances a theory of the electoral costs of exclusion, arguing that continued exclusion can become electorally costly when parties fail to adapt to changing electoral responses to women's representation. Using data from Spanish local elections (2003-2019) and a difference-in-differences design, we show that parties increasing women's representation in electable list positions gain votes and seats relative to parties that do not; this divergence coincides with gains among parties increasing women's representation and losses among those maintaining or reducing it. These consequences grow over time and are strongest where inclusion is voluntary rather than quota-mandated. Our findings challenge the idea that underrepresentation persists because inclusion fails electorally, pointing instead to a changing electoral constraint some elites may fail to recognize: exclusion has become costly.

articles.title: Still Secularizing: Cohort Replacement, Rebound, Overreporting, and Gender Convergence in a Pooled Analysis of Eight National Surveys
articles.abstract: Recent reports claim young men in the United States are becoming more religious. This would signal an end to the longstanding pattern of cohort-driven declines in religiosity. Pooling young-adult trends within eight national surveys measuring affiliation, attendance, salience, prayer, and biblical literalism, we find no measure shows a credible increase among young men, and the youngest cohort is no more religious than its predecessor was at the same age. The gender gap is narrowing because women are secularizing faster, not because men are returning, which likely reflects gender-based ideological realignment. Religiosity has rebounded from its pandemic trough, but not credibly past pre-pandemic levels, and the gap between self-reported attendance and time-use diaries has widened. Intense religious identity is also declining across cohorts. Variability between surveys, a post-pandemic rebound, and growing measurement drift are all confounding patterns of religious change. Cutting through the noise, cohort replacement continues to organize American religion.

articles.title: Daily Dynamics of Urban Racial Segregation in the United States
articles.abstract: This study examines racial segregation changes across the day and week to assess three perspectives in urban sociology: social isolation, compelled mobility, and cosmopolitanism. I link mobile phone tracking data collected on 18 days in January 2020 to 2020 Census data on the racial composition of estimated home tracts. Using the Theil multigroup segregation index, I estimate hourly racial segregation in 18 large U.S. commuting zones. Racial segregation is highest overnight, declines during weekday work hours, and is generally higher on weekends than weekdays. These patterns are most consistent with the compelled mobility perspective, under which lower racial segregation is expected when residents travel beyond their neighborhoods to access employment and other resources. Relatively high weekend racial segregation offers only weak support for social isolation. Friday and Saturday nights and the following early mornings have lower racial segregation than Wednesday at the same hours, offering clearer partial support for cosmopolitanism. Although the data do not identify why people travel, they show that the clearest declines in racial segregation coincide with the workday. Measuring racial segregation across hours and days thus helps distinguish theoretical accounts of how racial segregation persists or diminishes beyond residential neighborhoods.

articles.title: Health system and hospital utilization in Chile, 1952–2020: trends, reforms, and inflection points
articles.abstract: Objective. To collect and analyze longitudinal data on hospital discharges in Chile between 1952 and 2020, both at the national level and within the public subsystem. Patterns of change were identified in relation to the following key institutional milestones: the Curative Medicine Act of 1968, the creation of the National Health Services System in 1979, and the implementation of the Universal and Guaranteed Access Reform in 2005. Methods. A first-of-its-kind time series was constructed using official sources from the Ministry of Health and institutional documents. Indicators were calculated for the total number of discharges, discharge rates per thousand population, and comparisons with the United States. The analysis included exploratory graphics and construction of segmented regression models. Results. Hospital discharges rose steadily, with two periods mirroring robust expansion of the private sector: between 1982 and 1987 and between 2006 and 2019. Public provision of hospital services slowed or decreased with the 1979 reform and with the 2005 reform, although not with the 1968 reform. Conclusion. This study provides empirical evidence on the long-term trajectory of Chilean hospital services and confirms a structural contrast between the country's major health system models and the differences in their reforms. It also underscores the need for long-term information to analyze the impact of health reforms.

articles.title: Mind the Gap: Elite Preferences for Redistribution and How they Differ from the Mass Public
articles.authors: Mogens K. Justesen, Marko Klašnja, Sara Hobolt, Robert Klemmensen
articles.abstract: Increasing inequality has raised concerns over the disproportionate influence of the rich on public policies. Central to such concerns is the assumption that elite policy preferences are unified and differ significantly from the general public. We theorize economic elites as fiscal constituencies, highlighting intra-elite differences in policy preferences based on elite sources of affluence and therefore fiscal claims they face from the state. Employing high-quality administrative and survey data, including conjoint experiments, from Denmark, we compare tax and spending preferences in the general population with the largest samples to date of the top 1% by income and wealth. While elites are more economically conservative, they are not uniformly anti-redistribution; the asset-rich are less conservative than the income-rich; and their preferences often differ over tax policy. These findings highlight elite group differences based on their relation to the fiscal structure of the state and offer new insights into the micro-foundations of unequal representation in advanced democracies.

articles.title: Rethinking methods for studying online information and health decision-making: a participant-centred approach
articles.authors: NIHR Policy Research Unit in Reproductive Health, Elena Proffitt, Nicola Merrett, Lois Harvey-Pescott, Jennifer Hall, Abigail McNiven, Abimbola Ayorinde, Kamilla Abdullayev, Rebecca French, Kelly Dickson
articles.abstract: Online information, accessed through social media, websites, apps and artificial intelligence, is frequently described as shaping health attitudes and decision-making. Many methodological approaches to understanding how online information influences decisions provide important insights into online content, information exposure, or user perspectives, but often struggle to capture the personalised and algorithmically curated digital environments people encounter, how they engage with information as it appears in their everyday lives, and how such encounters intersect with wider social, cultural and personal contexts to shape decision making. New methodological approaches are needed that can generate meaningful evidence about the varied realities of navigating online health information and the role it plays in decision-making. Drawing on reproductive justice and feminist principles that privilege participant expertise and lived experience and informed by literature and collaboration with lived and learnt experts, we co-designed a participant-centred longitudinal content-oriented study exploring the influence of online information on contraceptive decision-making. Inspired by Photovoice approaches, participants documented in real time the online information they encountered over a one-month period, capturing content presented through their own tailored digital environments. Interviews conducted before and after the collection period explored contraceptive experiences, attitudes, decision-making and reflections on the role of online information. By combining real-time documentation with in-depth interviews, this approach enabled interpretations of participants lived encounters with online information, including algorithmic changes, emerging trends, current events, and the types of content that resonated with them. Collaborators with lived experience were involved throughout the methodological development and interpretation and analysis of findings. This participant-selected content-oriented longitudinal design demonstrates the value of methodologies that capture and generate evidence on lived digital and offline realities as they unfold in real time. Understanding how online information shapes health decision-making requires moving beyond approaches that treat the internet as an isolated and static influence on behaviours. Online information is not a singular, stable object of inquiry but dynamic, personalised, algorithmically mediated and embedded within broader social, cultural, and political contexts. Methodologies that recognise this complexity are essential for generating evidence capable of informing empathetic and meaningful health care and support and care for people prioritising their needs and navigating complex health decisions.

articles.title: A New Era of Political Socialization? The Interplay Between Political Social Media Exposure, Conspiracy Thinking, and Political Distrust Among Dutch Younger vs. Older Generations
articles.abstract: In recent years, populist radical-right parties (PRRP) have gained substantial electoral support in European countries, especially among younger voters. However, few studies have focused on the generational divide in PRRP voting behavior and the factors that explain why current younger generations are more likely to vote for PRRP. The current study addresses this research gap by examining whether generational differences in PRRP voting can be explained by variations in political social media exposure (PSME) and its indirect pathways through conspiracy thinking and political distrust, while accounting for the moderating role of anti-immigrant attitudes. Drawing on insights from developmental psychology, political psychology, and political science, we developed an interdisciplinary framework. We tested our expectations in the context of the Netherlands using data from the Dutch Parliamentary Election Study 2023, drawing on a sample of Dutch eligible voters. Results showed that current younger generations (Generations Y and Z) were more likely to vote for PRRP compared to older generations, partly explained by their higher PSME and subsequently, stronger conspiracy thinking and political distrust. Results further showed that the effect of conspiracy thinking on PRRP voting was particularly pronounced for respondents with low levels of anti-immigrant attitudes.

articles.title: Beyond Pathology: What Data Reveal about Radicalization and Prevention in a Parents4Peace Cohort
articles.authors: Megan K McBride, Jessica E. Stern, Michelle Strayer, Wilson Spurrell, Myrieme Churchill

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Research on trauma, mental distress, autism spectrum condition (ASD), and bullying among radicalized individuals has been inconclusive. To advance this discussion, our team coded 837 intervention notes associated with 65 persons whose families or friends engaged the services of Parents4Peace, an organization that offers guidance to individuals whose loved ones have radicalized or mobilized. ACE prevalence exceeded general baselines but remained below some extremist samples; mental distress/illness and ASD prevalence both exceeded general baselines and existing extremist samples; bullying exceeds general baselines. We attribute these findings, in part, to help-seeking, and as evidence of a complex radicalized population.

articles.title: "How do I survive the next 12 hours?": Disability and lived experiences of extreme heat in the UK
articles.authors: Hollye Kirkcaldy, Annayah M.B. Prosser, Keren MacLennan, Christina Demski

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: As extreme heat becomes a more frequent consequence of climate change, understanding how marginalised populations experience it is critical for adaptation. Disabled people are routinely categorised as ‘at-risk’, yet research largely quantifies heat risk at population level, leaving lived dimensions of heat experience for Disabled people under-explored, particularly in the UK. Drawing on theories of ableism and psycho-emotional disablism, this qualitative study asks how Disabled people in the UK experience extreme heat and what shapes their capacity to adapt. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 27 self-identified Disabled adults across the UK between July and September 2025 and analysed data using Reflexive Thematic Analysis. Across three main themes, participants depict heat as an actively disabling environmental condition which erodes capacity, diminishes identity, exposes ableist assumptions in adaptation and is mediated by material and structural conditions across housing, care and urban infrastructure. Current adaptation frameworks contain significant blind spots, including the temporal and psycho-emotional dimensions of heat harm, and are, in some respects, actively harmful for Disabled people. Addressing this requires a fundamental interrogation of whose knowledge informs the design of heat adaptation policy in the UK.

articles.title: Moral Load and Moral Strain: Situational Demands and the Experience of Carrying Them
articles.abstract: People often recognize that something morally significant is happening before they can name what they are experiencing. Existing vocabulary, including moral distress, moral injury, moral residue, and moral resilience, describes important forms and consequences of moral difficulty. This paper develops an analytic distinction among moral demands, moral load, and moral strain. Moral demands are the morally significant claims, obligations, risks, or consequences present in a situation. Moral load names how those demands bear on a particular person through roles, relationships, commitments, foreseeable consequences, and available agency; moral strain names the internal experience of carrying that load. Load is therefore neither a property of the situation alone nor a subjective reaction to it. Prior uses of moral load have addressed moral sensitivity, clinical decision-making, and moral deliberation. The contribution here is a relational architecture that separates situation-level demands, person-specific load, and internal strain. Demands, tasks, authority, resources, and support may be redistributed, thereby changing the load borne by particular people; support may also alter strain even when underlying load remains. Consequences including moral residue and moral injury can generate new obligations and shape later load and strain, making the relationship recursive rather than linear. Implications for education, team practice, and research are discussed.

articles.title: Observed Shifts in the Health Equity Research Landscape: Results of a National Survey of Health Equity Researchers April-July, 2025
articles.authors: Clair Kronk, Sima Rabinowitz, Denise Milstein, Devin Madden, Nita Vangeepuram, Dinushika Mohottige, Timnit Berhane, Andrew Maroko

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Objectives. To assess changes health equity researchers have made or anticipate making to their research in the context of the current federal administration’s policies on diversity, equity, and inclusion. Methods. We shared an electronic survey link with health equity researchers at academic, non-academic non-profit, non-academic for-profit, and governmental institutions in the U.S. between April and July 2025. 634 responses were received; 381 completed. The survey assessed demographics, occupational and institutional characteristics, perceptions of job security, experiences of stress, collaborations, censorship, and funding sources. Results. A large majority of respondents (96.6%) reported having made or anticipated making changes to their health equity research. Changes included: using different language (83.7.%), adapting or altering research questions (56.4%), pivoting to new health equity topics (49.6%), developing new health equity projects (50.4%), seeking new collaborators (31.0%), stopping health equity research activities (18.9%), and withdrawing from existing collaborations (8.9%). Conclusions. A significant number of health equity researchers have made or anticipate making fundamental changes to their research. These changes have critical implications for health equity research, public health, research teams, and the communities most impacted by this work.

articles.title: Efficiency, Elasticity, and Disruption: A Mechanistic Framework for Socio-Technical System Transitions
articles.authors: Vitor Miranda de Souza, Diogo Figueirinhas, Brian D. Fath, Fredrik Nilsson
articles.abstract: Efficiency improvements are persistently accompanied by demand expansion and increased resource throughput, systematically undermining sustainability strategies in operations and supply chain management. While existing explanations rely on behavioural assumptions or empirical correction factors rather than structural accounts, this paper develops a first-order mechanistic formulation of efficiency-induced demand expansion, introducing system elasticity εsys as a structural property of socio-technical configuration. Building on and generalising Ayres and Warr’s framework, we derive the service relationship S ∝ η^(ε_sys−1) and its resource corollary R ∝ η^(ε_sys−2), establishing two sustainability thresholds: ε_sys > 1 for service expansion and ε_sys > 2 for absolute resource growth. Two independent empirical cases – the 19th-century steam engine and contemporary computing – yield ε_sys ≈ 3.5, consistent with the backfire condition. The formulation reframes the operational challenge from governing resource efficiency to governing service elasticity.

articles.title: Post-growth policies and business transformation: A mixed-methods expert assessment of perceived relevance

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: This article examines how different policies are perceived by researchers regarding their relevance in supporting the transformation of traditional businesses toward reducing ecological footprints, securing well-being, and increasing social equity. While post-growth scholarship has discussed a wide range of policy proposals, their implications for business transformations remain underexplored. To address this gap, the study combines a quantitative survey of 1,734 sustainability policy researchers with qualitative focus group discussions with post-growth business scholars. The survey results indicate that the majority of policy instruments are perceived as at least moderately relevant for supporting a business transformation towards post-growth. Descriptive analyses show that respondents with a degrowth work-orientation tend to perceive the instruments as more relevant than growth-indifferent or green growth-oriented respondents, with differences particularly pronounced for more structurally disruptive interventions. The qualitative analysis explores how post-growth business scholars perceive key tensions, barriers, and enabling conditions associated with three previously highly ranked policies: transitioning ownership structures, banning planned obsolescence, and introducing declining resource caps. Two central topics emerge from these discussions: the role of businesses’ profit orientation as a structural factor that may shape responses to policy interventions, and the importance of combining policies in order to address anticipated tensions and wider societal implications. The article bridges post-growth policy and business research by suggesting how different policy instruments and mixes may support business transformations in line with post-growth objectives.

articles.title: When Red Is - and Is Not - Blood: A Corpus-Assisted Cognitive-Semantic Analysis of Five Settler Australian Texts (1874-1907)
articles.abstract: This study investigates when the colour term RED is conceptually connected with BLOOD and when the two domains remain independent in settler Australian literary discourse. The data comprise five complete public-domain texts published between 1874 and 1907 by Marcus Clarke, Henry Lawson, Miles Franklin, Joseph Furphy, and Jeannie Gunn. The study adopts a corpus-assisted qualitative design combining full-text lexical retrieval, paragraph-level concordance reading, cognitive-semantic annotation, and counterexample analysis. A verified analytical set of 30 concordance contexts was assembled across the five texts to test explicit BLOOD-RED bridges against competing RED and BLOOD pathways; the set is deliberately criterion-based and is not treated as a frequency sample. Three direct bridge types are attested: blood-red compounding, blood as a colour comparator, and bodily circulation as a causal basis for visible redness. The same texts also provide systematic counterevidence to any general RED IS BLOOD equation. RED occurs independently in landscape, fire, flora, atmospheric description, and conventional idioms, while BLOOD extends independently to violence, personhood, descent, temperament, inheritance, vitality, and exploitation. The findings support an asymmetrical partial-overlap model: BLOOD can motivate RED, but RED does not entail BLOOD, and many figurative BLOOD constructions have no chromatic component. The analysis further shows that red soil, red gum, and comparable Australian landscape expressions cannot be classified as blood imagery without local lexical or causal co-activation. Methodologically, the study demonstrates the value of separating lexical semantics, metonymic motivation, metaphorical extension, and literary symbolism before cross-linguistic comparison.

articles.title: Geopolitical Influence & Peace: Tracking the trends shaping international relations
articles.abstract: This report asks whether the world has entered a "new Cold War" and what intensifying great power competition means for peace, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Using datasets including SIPRI, ICEWS, UCDP/PRIO, the Correlates of War and the Foreign Bilateral Influence Capability (FBIC) dataset, it compares today's international system with the Cold War and post-Cold War periods. Geopolitical risk now exceeds Cold War levels and is nearing the peaks seen after 9/11. Global military expenditure reached a record US$2.43 trillion in 2023, the largest annual rise since 2009. Nuclear disarmament has stalled, and the UN Security Council has become less effective, with fewer resolutions passed and more vetoes since the 2010s. Bilateral sentiment between the US, Russia and China has deteriorated since 1995. The current system nonetheless differs from the Cold War. It is multipolar and economically interdependent, although trade has plateaued at around 60 per cent of global GDP. It is also shaped by technological competition and global challenges such as climate change. The number of countries holding more than 10 per cent influence in five or more other states has almost tripled, from 13 at the end of the Cold War to 34 in 2024. This reflects the rise of middle powers such as Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, Brazil, South Africa, Vietnam and Indonesia, alongside China and India. For LMICs, competition for influence is intensifying, notably in the Sahel, West Africa, South Asia and South America. The US holds more than 10 per cent influence in 74 LMICs and China in 65. China is dominant in sub-Saharan Africa and the US in Latin America. Internationalised intrastate conflicts have increased nearly threefold since 2010. The Sudan and Syria case studies show how external backing for warring parties can prolong conflict and raise the risk of mass atrocities. Proxy wars also drove many of the Cold War's deadliest conflicts. Economic pressures compound these risks. In 2024, 3.3 billion people lived in countries where debt interest payments exceeded spending on health and education. Aid is also shifting from multilateral to bilateral channels, which further constrains development and Positive Peace. The report concludes that competition for influence can undermine local governance and divert attention from climate change, food insecurity and peacebuilding. A nuanced understanding of these dynamics is needed to support long-term stability and development in the developing world.

articles.title: No King, and Other Matters—America’s Perspectives in Mid-2026 on Democracy, Authoritarianism, and Election-Related Violence: Findings from a Nationally Representative Survey
articles.authors: Garen Wintemute, Bradley Velasquez, Sonia Robinson, Krista Neumann, Shaina Sta Cruz, Aaron Shev, Daniel Tancredi, Elizabeth A. Tomsich, Mona A. Wright, Veronica Pear

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Background: Political violence and the rise of authoritarianism are emerging threats to the nation’s health, stability, and future as a representative democracy. To inform and facilitate prevention efforts, we present new and updated findings on the public’s views on authoritarianism and its support for and willingness to engage in election-related and pro- or anti-government violence. Methods: Findings are from Wave 5, conducted May 15-June 15, 2026, of a nationally representative annual longitudinal survey of adult members of the Ipsos KnowledgePanel that was initiated in 2022. Findings are for the cohort as a whole and for subgroups defined by political party/Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement affiliation. Year-to-year change for items included in 2025 and 2026 is estimated using mean change scores. Cross-sectional findings for 2026 are presented as weighted prevalences and item scores. Results: The completion rate was 90.7%; there were 7,552 respondents. Nearly 90% of respondents continued to consider it very or extremely important that the US remain a democracy (change 0.01, 95% CI -0.00, 0.03). Agreement with expressions of authoritarianism was much less common; it decreased for the statement, “having a strong leader for America is more important than having a democracy” (change -0.04, 95% CI -0.07, -0.02) and others. In 2026, 2.1% (95% CI 1.6%, 2.7%) of respondents agreed strongly or very strongly that President Trump should be made king, but nearly half (47.7%, 95% CI 46.2%, 49.2%) agreed strongly or very strongly that he should be impeached and removed from office. There was little agreement with 5 actions the federal government might take in 2026 that employed violence to enforce its policies or suppress its critics in the US; the prevalence of strong or very strong agreement ranged between 4.4% and 9.6%. Across 12 items, there was very little agreement with actions—including violence—the federal government might take to subvert elections; strong or very strong agreement ranged between 2% and 4%. Willingness to commit violence was rare. For example, only 1.6% (95% CI 1.2%, 2.1%) were very or completely willing to use violence “to make sure that President Trump remains in office after his term ends.” Decreases from 2025 to 2026 in support for expressions of authoritarianism and for government-initiated violence were common across the spectrum of party/MAGA movement affiliations. Conclusions: With national elections a few months away, Americans remained strongly supportive of democracy, did not endorse authoritarianism, and rejected the use of force by the current federal government to enforce its policies or subvert elections. They were deeply unwilling to engage in violence. These hopeful findings can inform and guide efforts to preserve democracy and prevent political violence.

articles.title: Adolescent Online Leisure, Media Literacy, and Emotional Distress from Online Victimization: Evidence Across Fifty Countries and Economies
articles.authors: Yunqi Wang, Yan Ruth Xia, James A. Bovaird, Maria Rosario T. de Guzman, Paul Springer, Xiaoran Sun
articles.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has accelerated adolescents’ engagement in online activities. However, research on adolescents’ technology use and mental health often overlooks the complexity of online behaviors and the role of media literacy without examining specific mechanisms. This study addresses the gap by analyzing survey data from 295,843 adolescents aged 15-16 years across 50 countries and economies from Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA) collected in 2022, examining the relations among adolescent online leisure, media literacy, and emotional distress from online victimization. Structural equation modeling results revealed that both adolescents’ online leisure and media literacy are positively associated with their emotional distress from online victimization experiences, such as exposure to unwanted content. Findings provide important implications for research, theories, and practices, highlighting an urgent need for parenting practices and interventions to promote adolescents’ media literacy and digital skills to navigate the online environment and mitigate online risks.

articles.title: Effective Anti-Corruption Strategies for Public Organizations: Insights from Meta-Analysis and Meta-Regression

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Fighting corruption remains one of the most pressing management challenges in public organizations worldwide. While different organizational approaches to anti‑corruption exist, evidence of their effectiveness and the conditions under which they reduce different forms of administrative corruption remains limited. Drawing on a meta analysis and meta regression of 174 effect sizes from 34 empirical studies, this study shows that both integrity based and compliance based anti corruption strategies have a significant, positive, small to moderate effect on public organizations’ ethical performance, although their effectiveness varies across contexts. Compliance based strategies, particularly formalization and accountability mechanisms, are more effective in addressing multiple forms of administrative corruption, whereas integrity‑based strategies, such as ethical leadership, primarily reduce collusion, demonstrating that ‘one-size-fits-all’ approaches are ineffective. The findings highlight the conditional effectiveness of organizational anti‑corruption strategies and the importance of context‑sensitive ethics management. These findings carry important implications for public administration theory, research, and practice.

articles.title: Adverse Outcomes Among Youths Admitted to Compulsory Institutional Care: A Swedish Matched Cohort Study
articles.authors: Amber L. Beckley, Fredrik Sivertsson, Sofi Oskarsson, Catherine Tuvblad, Peter Larm
articles.abstract: Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care represent a particularly vulnerable population with substantial behavioral, social, and health-related needs. However, evidence on their long-term outcomes relative to other high-risk youths, and on when adverse outcomes emerge following discharge, remains limited. We examined the characteristics of youths admitted to compulsory institutional care in Sweden, compared their overall and adulthood outcomes with matched youths from the general population and compulsory social care, and examined the timing of adverse outcomes following discharge. The Swedish Longitudinal Compulsory Care Study (SLCCS) includes all youths admitted to compulsory institutional care (CIC) in Sweden between 2000 and 2020 (n = 14,677), matched to youths from the general population (14,349 pairs) and compulsory social care (8,879 pairs). Analyses were stratified by sex and included descriptive statistics, fixed-effects regression, Cox proportional hazards models, and Kaplan–Meier analyses. Criminal behavior and substance use were the most common reasons for placement. The CIC group experienced poorer outcomes than both comparison groups overall and in adulthood. Compared with matched women from the general population, adjusted hazards of substance use disorder (HR = 7.83, 95% CI 6.07–10.10) and all-cause mortality (HR = 8.42, 95% CI 3.01–23.54) were nearly eightfold higher among women admitted to compulsory institutional care. Corresponding hazards among men were fivefold higher for substance use disorder (HR = 5.11, 95% CI 4.26–6.12) and threefold higher for all-cause mortality (HR = 3.11, 95% CI 2.02–4.77). Kaplan–Meier analyses indicated that mental health and substance use diagnoses were concentrated within the first five years following discharge. Youths admitted to compulsory institutional care face an elevated risk of adverse outcomes extending into adulthood, and the first five years following discharge may represent an important period for aftercare and support.

articles.title: Social Exclusion, Institutional Support and the Perceived Criminal Involvement of Waste Pickers: Evidence from a Stakeholder Survey in Rawalpindi–Islamabad, Pakistan

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Informal waste pickers (rag-pickers) are among the most marginalised urban groups in Pakistan, yet they are often linked in public debate to petty crime, substance use and sex work. This study surveys 300 frontline stakeholders (78 police personnel, 175 NGO staff and 47 other residents) in Rawalpindi and Islamabad to examine which offences they attribute to waste pickers and how these perceptions relate to perceived social exclusion and perceived support from government and NGOs. Substance use (80%) and prostitution (79%) were the offences most often attributed; murder rarely (5%). Perceived social exclusion was strongly associated with perceived criminal involvement (r = .73, p < .001), while perceived institutional support showed a weak negative association (r = -.17, p = .004). In a regression model (R2 = .53), exclusion was the only significant predictor (beta = .75); the association of support with criminal involvement operated indirectly through lower exclusion (indirect effect = -.23, Sobel z = -5.27, p < .001). The findings suggest that support reduces perceived criminality only insofar as it reduces exclusion, and argue for inclusion-oriented policy: integrating waste pickers into municipal waste systems, making social protection reachable, and protective rather than extractive policing. Based on the author's MPhil thesis (National Defence University, Islamabad, 2020).

articles.title: Fear of coordination costs can increase conservative attitudes
articles.abstract: Why individuals sometimes defend social orders that hurt their interests is a fundamental question in the social sciences. Leading accounts emphasize loss aversion or needs to justify established social systems as the main explanations. Across two pre-registered experiments with U.S. respondents, we explored the hypothesis that attachment to an established social convention (the status quo) when facing better alternatives is driven by fear of miscoordination and perceived transition costs. Experiment 1 shows that when a third party institution can step in to ensure a new coordination equilibrium is reached, people become less attached to a suboptimal status quo. With Experiment 2, we show that a greater diversity of preferences within a population increases attachment to the status quo, consistent with the view that the perceived difficulty of coordinating on a new equilibrium makes the status quo attractive. Both hypotheses were supported across a large array of issues involving coordination of multiple individuals, from rules regulating nuclear weapon use to software use to religious rituals in small scale societies. Our paper provides experimental proof that fear of miscoordination can suffice to motivate people to remain conservative with respect to suboptimal social institutions in the presence of better alternatives.

articles.title: Citizen Trust in AI Regulatory Regimes in Four EU Countries

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) applications is deemed crucial for uptake of the technology and the development of an AI market. In the present article, we argue that the institutional design of regulatory regimes matters for whether citizens trust AI systems. We study how trust in AI systems depends on who the responsible regulator is, the scope of the regulator’s scrutiny of AI systems, and the involvement of external stakeholders in regulatory oversight. Based on a conjoint design, we examine how respondents value these institutional design choices for the case of high-risk AI systems used in health care. Using samples from Lithuania, Romania, Sweden, and the Netherlands, with 4001 respondents overall, the pre-registered experiment shows that citizens have more trust in AI systems if vendors, civil society and especially independent researchers are involved in oversight, and if regulators actively scrutinize AI systems rather than relying solely on self-reporting. At least in two countries, citizens also seem to have more trust in AI systems if the sectoral health care regulator is the responsible regulator instead of a cross-sectoral regulator such as the national Data Protection Authority or a specific AI regulator.

articles.title: The distinctive nature of non-partisanship: How independents pursue and prioritize political information
articles.abstract: The two major parties present American voters with increasingly stark electoral alternatives. How do independents make political decisions in this era of heightened partisanship? Prevailing accounts portray independents either as inattentive, low-information voters or as "undercover" partisans whose behavior mirrors that of Democrats and Republicans. We challenge both characterizations. Drawing on novel survey experiments, we compare the information-seeking behavior of independents and partisans by examining the importance they attach to different candidate attributes and the quantity of information they seek before choosing between candidates. We find that independents and partisans rank candidate attributes in similar ways, with both groups prioritizing issue positions over socio-demographic characteristics. Yet, independents rely less on candidate partisanship and acquire more information than partisans across a variety of hypothetical electoral conditions. These differences persist across levels of political knowledge, suggesting that independents and partisans use distinct decision rules when evaluating political candidates.

articles.title: Beyond compensation: Climate politics, mobilization, and transformative statecraft
articles.abstract: Governments have pursued decarbonization through a combination of subsidies for capital and compensation for people. Political scientists have identified the compensation of those who incur losses from climate policies as the the central challenge in building green coalitions and achieving a just transition. However, a decarbonization path aimed at limiting global warming to 2 degrees Celsius entails transformative change for virtually everyone. We argue that, under such conditions, a compensation-based approach reduces green backlash to pocketbook concerns; citizens to bundles of fixed preferences; and evaluation to policy-by-policy assessment. Proposing to move beyond compensating existing preferences, we contend that transformative statecraft reshapes preferences through political mobilization. From this perspective, a technocratic approach—focused on calculation and compensation—constitutes a binding constraint on green statecraft. We defend this mobilization-based approach against the objections of manipulation and deprivation of freedom and suggest that a democratic version of transformative statecraft is possible.

articles.title: Language Replacement and Individualism: Linguicide as a Measurable Cultural Variable
articles.abstract: Cross-cultural research has linked grammatical features, especially the obligatory use of subject pronouns, to national individualism, but such links are hard to separate from language family, wealth and history. This study treats colonial language replacement as a measurable variable and asks whether colonized countries whose majority home language became a European colonizer's language are more individualist than colonized countries that kept their own. Using a 55-country dataset and a validated individualism index (Akaliyski et al., 2025), I compare 10 replaced-language and 9 retained-language countries, controlling for GDP and diagnostic infrastructure. Replacement was associated with 12.1 points higher individualism (95% CI [8.0, 16.2]). The association was larger where English, which requires overt subject pronouns, did the replacing (17.5 points) than where Spanish or Portuguese, which allow pronoun drop, did so (11.4 points), though the difference between the two was not statistically significant (p = .10). The replacement association persisted when census-based settler population share was controlled, and settler share showed no independent association. This test rests largely on a single case: Ireland, where the population remained and the language shifted, scored with the English-speaking settler states. Within Ireland (N = 3,057), residents of areas where more Irish was spoken in 1911 placed less weight on self-direction values today, while present-day daily use of Irish showed no association. Within Latin America, Indigenous language retention was inversely associated with individualism, but this could not be separated from national wealth. Replacement was not associated with autism prevalence once diagnostic capacity was controlled. I argue that language replacement offers a direct, measurable proxy for linguicide and a route for testing claims about language and selfhood.

articles.title: From volume to care: an ethic of aver cura for tourism and host-community well-being
articles.authors: Christian Josef Wiedermann, Patrick Rina, Harald Pechlaner, Fulvio Longato

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Purpose. This paper proposes an ethic of care — aver cura — as an integrative concept for destination development that connects two disconnected uses of "care" in tourism scholarship and specifies how the concept can be observed and measured. Design/methodology/approach. The paper is conceptual. It synthesizes tourism studies, public health and the ethics of care, and illustrates the argument through the single case of Meran, South Tyrol, a historic alpine health resort. Findings. Tourism research invokes care as an ethos, while public health and health tourism treat care as provision; the two seldom meet. An ethic of aver cura, built on caring for self, others and place, integrates them and reframes success from volume to sustaining visitor, resident, worker and landscape together. Civic trust, distinct from commercial destination trust, is the operational core through which care becomes measurable. Research limitations/implications. The six propositions are conceptual and untested; they set a future agenda for comparative and longitudinal research. Practical implications. Destinations would shift from volume metrics to civic-trust and community indicators and to recurring deliberative governance. Social implications. The approach foregrounds the well-being of residents and tourism workers alongside that of visitors. Originality/value. The paper offers an integrative concept of care that bridges ethical and public-health registers, distinguishes civic from commercial trust as its measurable core, and grounds care in a destination's own formative logic rather than importing it from outside. Preprint of a manuscript currently under review at the Journal of Tourism Futures (Emerald). This is the submitted version and has not been peer-reviewed.

articles.title: Making Place for Health and Good Life: Tourism at the Intersection of Philosophy and Public Health
articles.authors: Fulvio Longato, Patrick Rina, Christian Josef Wiedermann

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Tourism is increasingly promoted as a resource for health, and destinations market the well-being their landscapes are said to afford; yet the notion of well-being invoked where tourism and public health meet requires further specification, as the fields that converge there do not necessarily use the term in the same sense. The conceptual analysis clarifies well-being by distinguishing its psychological dimensions from its philosophical characterisation in terms of human flourishing, and frames health from a salutogenic perspective. Human flourishing and salutogenesis intersect particularly through meaningfulness and the ways persons engage with what places make possible. Drawing on the phenomenology of the tourist experience and on the literatures of therapeutic landscapes and restorative environments, the paper argues that places contribute to health through multiple and potentially interacting pathways involving characteristics of settings, activities and experiences, and their social and environmental contexts. Embodied pathways further show the interconnection of experiential and bodily dimensions of health. The paper draws out implications for public health and participatory destination design. Alpine tourism destinations provide a suitable context in which these relationships can be examined empirically.

articles.title: Patient-reported experience as audit evidence: a new perspective on governance in integrated care

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Patient-reported experience can identify problems in integrated care, yet feedback alone does not show whether organisations address them. This Perspective argues that experience data can inform internal audit evidence and person-centred healthcare governance when their quality, context and interpretive limits are examined. Developed within the author's doctoral research programme, the argument draws on a purposively selected set of scientific publications and official documents; it does not report a literature review or analyse the programme's empirical datasets. The conceptual method compares the purposes and units of patient-experience measurement, SCIROCCO integration maturity assessment, value-based healthcare implementation assessment and professional internal audit. An illustrative crosswalk then connects five coordination and participation concerns with contextual domains, candidate audit questions, corroborating information and management follow-up. The proposed cycle moves from patient-defined priorities through evidence evaluation to accountable action and repeated assessment of experience. It preserves management ownership of controls and distinguishes a reported concern from a demonstrated organisational failure. Neither the crosswalk nor the combined framework has been empirically validated. Patient involvement, feasibility assessment and comparative evaluation are needed to establish usefulness, burden and effects. The contribution is a testable governance proposition, not evidence of improved clinical outcomes or economic value. Keywords: patient-reported experience data, internal audit, audit evidence, integrated care, SCIROCCO maturity model, healthcare governance, person-centred care

articles.title: Maternal Solidarity: Unconditional Cash Prescriptions and a Moral Economy of Motherhood in Flint, Michigan
articles.authors: Caroline Doenmez, Jenny LaChance, Mallory Goldsworthy, Mona Hanna

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: How do mothers make meaning out of the experience of being “prescribed” no-strings-attached cash to improve their family’s health and life chances? This paper explores the impact of Rx Kids, the first community-wide cash transfer program for mothers and newborns in the United States. Launched in Flint, Michigan, in January 2024, the program seeks to “prescribe away” child poverty by providing cash transfers to mothers during and after their pregnancies. The program design stands apart from other cash transfer programs due to its universal and unconditional features: it ensures that all pregnant mothers in a participating community can receive the cash and does not impose any spending restrictions or reporting requirements on them. This paper is interested in Rx Kids’ cultural impact as ascertained through mothers’ narratives of their involvement with the program. Drawing on 46 interviews conducted with mothers in Flint, we ask: What did the unconditionality and universality of the program mean to them? Through their narratives, we identify how the transfer of monetary resources to the mothers elicited profound moral considerations. As mothers moved through the process of encountering, applying to, participating in, and advocating for the program, they narrated grappling continuously with the question of maternal worth and worthiness. Through their affective experiences of disbelief, astonishment, mistrust, anxiety, gratitude, and compassion for other mothers, we argue that the participants give voice to a moral economy of motherhood in Flint, circulating and contesting cultural values regarding reproductive labor and maternal worth. Ultimately, we show how through participating in the program, the mothers were actualized as both the recipients and providers of what we term “maternal solidarity,” an unconditional mode of care premised on a shared understanding of the pronounced and ubiquitous challenges of contemporary motherhood.

articles.title: Blaming Across the Aisle: Political Contrasting and Blame Attribution in the Danish Parliament
articles.authors: Markus Lundsfryd Jensen, Rune Egeskov Trust, Kenneth C. Enevoldsen, Sara Kolding
articles.abstract: Political discourse is widely perceived to be growing more hostile, yet robust evidence remains scarce. This study examines blame attribution in the Danish Parliament from 1997 to 2026, combining a purpose-built classifier, BlameBERT (F1: 0.80), with multilevel statistical modeling. The classifier is constructed using an annotation-efficient pipeline for blame attribution in low-to-mid resource languages. The results reveal a banana-shaped trajectory, with blame declining until around 2016 before entering a significant and sustained increase in recent years (2019-2026). Government status consistently influenced blame attribution - an effect we term political contrasting - with opposition parties blaming substantially more than governing parties. This effect was moderated by ideology: The blame-dampening effect of governing was less pronounced among right-wing parties, and ideological extremity amplified blame more strongly on the right. In recent years, the interaction between political wing and ideological extremity intensified, suggesting an ideological hardening of the blame rhetoric concentrated on the right of the political spectrum. Taken together, these patterns suggest that the perceived rise in harsh political language reflects not merely a general rhetorical drift, but an ideologically asymmetric hardening of political discourse. A sensitivity analysis showed that the conclusions were robust to varying classification thresholds.

articles.title: FRAGMENTED GOVERNANCE AND THE FAILURE TO EXECUTE URBAN PROJECTS: THE LARGO DA BATATA COMPETITION (2001-2022)
articles.abstract: Architecture and urban design competitions are often defended as democratic selection mechanisms, yet many fail during implementation. This article argues the failure stems from fragmented governance: semi-autonomous sectoral authorities operating without a coordinating hierarchy. Through a 21-year documentary analysis of the National Competition for the Urban Reconversion of Largo da Batata (São Paulo), comparing the winning, basic and executed projects (2001-2022), we show each authority discharged its mandate competently, yet the absence of coordination fragmented the outcome. This mechanism, pockets of micro-regulation practices, moves the debate from describing competition failure to explaining it, with implications for governance research.

articles.title: Heed the warning: how NATO can find and fill the gaps in its warning systems

subjects.name: Public Affairs, Public Policy and Public Administration

articles.abstract: Intelligence warning failures are too often viewed in binary: Either intelligence succeeded or it failed. In reality, often only segments of the warning chain collapse while others operate well. This Outlook paper treats warning success as a spectrum rather than as a pass/fail test in a new framework for warning performance. It illustrates the use through three recent case studies: the fall of Kabul (2021), Russia’s invasion of Ukraine (2022) and the Niger coup (2023). The decisive shortfall across all three cases was the failure to reconcile divergent NATO member state views into an operational consensus within NATO. There are practical solutions for integrating NATO capabilities to institutionalize rapid after-action reviews, conduct periodic divergence drill exercises, prepare contingency packages and further embed red team analyses.
